docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Generated by make_logo.py.

JAXScape is a minimal JAX library for connectivity modelling at scale. It provides the building blocks of a connectivity analysis workflow:

  • differentiable and GPU-accelerated distances on graphs
  • differentiable raster-to-graph and graph-to-raster mappings
  • moving-window utilities for connectivity analyses of large rasters

JAXScape runs on CPUs, GPUs and TPUs through JAX. Its computations are differentiable, for sensitivity analysis and optimization, and it implements its own linear solvers and differentiation rules where JAX provides none.

Speed-up: the smallest speed-up of JAXScape on one GPU over another package in the benchmark of JAXScape 0.0.16, that is, the warm runtime of the package divided by that of JAXScape, each in its fastest setting on the largest synthetic raster that both completed, with JAXScape under the distance or setting with which the benchmark compares the package. The benchmark page of the documentation details the comparison.

ilg-toolkit builds on JAXScape for inverse landscape genetics, the inference of landscape permeability from geolocated molecular data. It works with the JAX scientific machine learning ecosystem, including Equinox and Flax, whose layers can be used to build neural networks that map landscape features to permeability. ResistanceGA (genetic algorithm) and radish (gradient-based optimization) address the same problem.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
uv add jaxscape

The default installation is CPU-only. For NVIDIA GPUs, use uv add 'jaxscape[cuda]', or install JAX following the official JAX installation guide. JAXScape will automatically use the JAX backend you have configured.

Least-cost path and resistance distances on rasters work with the default installation. Free-energy distances on large rasters, and resistance or free-energy distances on large graphs that are not rasters, such as networks of habitat patches, need an optional linear solver. See Linear solvers.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Download sample data

curl -sL https://github.com/vboussange/jaxscape/releases/download/v0.0.6/data.zip -o data.zip && unzip -q data.zip && rm data.zip

2. Run the analysis

import jax.numpy as jnp
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
from jaxscape import FreeEnergyDistance, GridGraph, LCPDistance, ResistanceDistance

permeability = jnp.array(
    np.loadtxt("data/permeability.csv", delimiter=","), dtype=jnp.float32
) + 0.01
barriers = np.asarray(permeability <= 0.1)

# Symmetric conductances are the mean permeability of neighbouring cells.
grid = GridGraph(grid=permeability, fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)

# Compute distances from the top-left pixel to every other pixel.
source = grid.coord_to_index(jnp.array([0]), jnp.array([0]))
distances = {
    "Least-cost path": LCPDistance()(grid, sources=source),
    "Resistance": ResistanceDistance()(grid, sources=source),
    r"Free energy, $\theta = 0.03$": FreeEnergyDistance(theta=0.03)(grid, sources=source),
}

distance_cmap = plt.cm.magma.copy()
distance_cmap.set_bad(color="lightgray")

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(12, 3.3))

permeability_im = axs[0].imshow(permeability, cmap="gray", vmin=0, vmax=1)
axs[0].set_xticks([])
axs[0].set_yticks([])
for spine in axs[0].spines.values():
    spine.set_visible(True)
axs[0].set_title("Permeability")
fig.colorbar(permeability_im, ax=axs[0], shrink=0.2)

for ax, (title, dist_to_node) in zip(axs[1:], distances.items()):
    # Convert from node values to a 2D array and hide barrier cells
    dist_array = np.asarray(grid.node_values_to_array(dist_to_node.ravel()))
    dist_array = np.ma.masked_where(barriers, dist_array)

    # Plotting
    im = ax.imshow(dist_array, cmap=distance_cmap)
    ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title)
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, shrink=0.2)

fig.suptitle("Distance from the top-left pixel")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

theta is the inverse temperature of the free-energy distance: larger values bring it closer to the least-cost path distance. For other graphs and larger landscapes, see Linear solvers for the choice of solver.

These distances are differentiable: jax.grad of a scalar function of them, such as their mean, gives its derivative with respect to the permeability of every pixel. The distance calculation example maps this derivative.

docs.title: Connectivity analysis
docs.text: ConnectivityAnalysis computes the connectivity of a landscape raster: the sum of the proximities of its pairs of pixels, weighted by their habitat quality, where the proximity of two pixels is a decreasing function of their distance. SensitivityAnalysis computes the derivatives of this connectivity with respect to the quality and the permeability of each pixel. Both compute distances window by window: the memory of their distance computations is set by dependency_range and batch_size, independent of the raster size. The window operations serve to build other definitions of connectivity (see Window operations).

docs.title: Windowed analyses
docs.text: ConnectivityAnalysis and SensitivityAnalysis subclass WindowedAnalysis: they share its arguments, and its windows, coarsening, tiles, padding and permeability floor.

docs.title: jaxscape.windowed_analysis.WindowedAnalysis
docs.text:
Base class for windowed connectivity analyses on large rasters.

Every pixel is the centre of a window of 2 * dependency_range + 1 pixels a side, and forms pairs with the pixels of its window only. The rasters are padded so that the windows of the pixels at the raster edges fit: the padding has quality 0 and the permeability floor. Permeability below the floor, 1e-4 times the maximum permeability, is raised to it: the graph of every window is connected, and regions of zero permeability stay nearly impassable.

With coarsening, only the windows of block centres are computed, every b pixels along each axis and on the first and last pixels, where b is dependency_range * coarsening_factor rounded up to an odd integer. Values between block centres are interpolated bilinearly: the weight of a centre falls linearly from 1 at the centre to 0 at the neighbouring centres, along each axis, and the weights of all centres sum to 1 at every pixel.

Block centres run in batches of at most batch_size. Distances whose queries from several sources share work, such as ResistanceDistance (see AbstractDistance.sources_share_work), compute a batch on tiles: a tile is the union of the windows of a grid of block centres, and one query on it gives each centre its distances to the pixels of its window. The graph of a tile extends beyond each window, so that the distances computed on it are lower than those computed on the window alone, and sensitivity maps have seams along the edges between tiles. Larger tiles cost less per block centre and leave fewer seams. Other distances, such as LCPDistance, compute the distances of each block centre on its own window. Randomized distances, such as ResistanceDistance with SpielmanApproximation, apply the proximity returned by AbstractDistance.debiased_proximity.

An analysis builds its solver states once, and every run starts from them and reuses the compiled programs (see Reusing solver state).

Arguments:

  • quality_raster: Habitat quality values. Both rasters take their common dtype, which is floating, and so do the results: an integer or boolean quality takes the floating dtype of the permeability, and a float32 raster with a float64 one gives float64.
  • permeability_raster: Movement permeability, or function quality -> permeability. An integer or boolean permeability takes JAX's default floating dtype.
  • distance: Distance, such as LCPDistance() or ResistanceDistance().
  • dependency_range: Window half-width D in pixels. Pairs farther apart than D along either axis do not contribute, and the default proximity decays over D / 4 equivalent pixels.
  • batch_size: Largest number of block centres per batch, which sets the memory: a batch holds its windows, or the distances that the queries on its tiles return. Exact ResistanceDistance and FreeEnergyDistance hold m * n distances for m sources and n tile vertices, besides the memory of the solver. With batch_size at least the number of block centres, one tile covers the raster.
  • proximity: Function mapping distances, in the units of distance, to proximities. Defaults to exp(-r / (D / 4)), where r is the distance in equivalent pixels: the number of pixels through habitat of permeability 1 that gives the same distance. See ConnectivityAnalysis for the units of each distance and the ecological rationale.
  • coarsening_factor: Coarsening, in [0, 1]. Block centres lie b pixels apart, for b equal to dependency_range * coarsening_factor rounded up to an odd integer. 0 computes the window of every pixel; larger values compute fewer windows, and run faster.

Example

The subclasses share these arguments:

from jaxscape import (
    ConnectivityAnalysis,
    ResistanceDistance,
    SensitivityAnalysis,
)

settings = dict(
    quality_raster=quality,
    permeability_raster=permeability,
    distance=ResistanceDistance(),  # GeometricMultigridCGSolver
    dependency_range=20,
    batch_size=100,
    coarsening_factor=0.25,  # blocks of 5 x 5 pixels
)
connectivity = ConnectivityAnalysis(**settings).run()
d_permeability = SensitivityAnalysis(**settings).run("permeability")

docs.title: jaxscape.connectivity_analysis.ConnectivityAnalysis
docs.text:
Connectivity of a landscape raster: the sum of the proximities of its pairs of pixels.

With quality weights, the connectivity is

\[C = \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} q_i \, K_{ij} \, q_j\]

where \(q_i\) is habitat quality at pixel \(i\) and \(K_{ij}\) is the proximity between pixels \(i\) and \(j\), a function proximity of their distance \(d_{ij}\) computed in the window centred on pixel \(i\), or in a tile that holds it (see WindowedAnalysis). Pairs farther apart than dependency_range \(D\) along either axis do not contribute.

By default, \(K_{ij} = e^{-r_{ij}/\alpha}\) with \(\alpha = D/4\), where \(r_{ij}\) is the distance in equivalent pixels: the number of pixels through habitat of permeability 1 that gives the distance \(d_{ij}\). This is the negative-exponential dispersal kernel of metapopulation theory (Hanski & Ovaskainen, 2000). In two dimensions, its mean dispersal distance is \(2\alpha = D/2\), and 91 % of its mass lies within distance \(4\alpha = D\) of the source.

With coarsening, each pixel takes the term \(\sum_{j \neq c} K_{cj} q_j\) of block centres \(c\), interpolated with the weights \(T_c(i)\) of WindowedAnalysis:

\[C \approx \sum_c \Big(\sum_i T_c(i) \, q_i\Big) \sum_{j \neq c} K_{cj} \, q_j\]

The pairs of pixels within a block contribute to this sum, so that it needs no calibration.

The analysis computes distances window by window, so that its memory does not grow with the size of the raster. See WindowedAnalysis for the windows, coarsening, padding at the raster edges and the permeability floor.

Distance units

A custom proximity receives distances in the units of distance:

  • EuclideanDistance: pixels.
  • LCPDistance: the sum of the edge costs 1 / a along the path, for the conductance a of each edge, the mean permeability of its two pixels; hence pixels at permeability 1.
  • ResistanceDistance: effective resistance, with edge resistances 1 / a. It grows like the logarithm of the pixel distance: at permeability 1 in a window of 41 pixels a side, it is 0.50, 1.28 and 1.89 at 1, 10 and 20 pixels from the centre. A kernel exp(-d / c) of the resistance therefore decays as a power law in pixels, and the window edge sets its range.
  • FreeEnergyDistance: from the least-cost path distance (large theta) to a multiple of the resistance (small theta).

When the analysis is created, the default proximity reads equivalent pixels off one window of permeability 1: the distances from its centre along an axis, interpolated linearly between pixels and in proportion past the window edge. Randomized distances read them off the exact distances that they estimate (see AbstractDistance.exact). For EuclideanDistance and LCPDistance, \(r_{ij} = d_{ij}\). Scale permeability so that 1 is optimal habitat.

Example

from jaxscape import ConnectivityAnalysis, LCPDistance

conn = ConnectivityAnalysis(
    quality_raster=quality,
    permeability_raster=permeability,
    distance=LCPDistance(),
    dependency_range=20,  # Window half-width in pixels
    batch_size=1000,
)
connectivity_index = conn.run(q_weighted=True)

Contiguity

The graph connects each pixel to its four neighbours along the rows and columns (rook contiguity), and the weight of each edge is the mean permeability of its two pixels.

Compute the connectivity metric across the landscape.

Arguments:

  • q_weighted: If True, weight each pair of pixels by their habitat qualities. If False, sum the proximities alone, with \(q_i = 1\) inside the raster.

Returns:

docs.title: jaxscape.connectivity_analysis.SensitivityAnalysis
docs.text:
Sensitivity of connectivity to the quality or permeability of each pixel.

Returns \(\partial C / \partial q_i\) or \(\partial C / \partial p_i\): how the connectivity \(C\) of ConnectivityAnalysis responds to the habitat quality or permeability of each pixel. Parameters, distance units and the default proximity are those of ConnectivityAnalysis.

Without coarsening, the result is the gradient of ConnectivityAnalysis.run with the same arguments, computed by automatic differentiation. With SpielmanApproximation, the gradient with respect to permeability is computed from an estimate of the gradient of the exact resistances (see ResistanceDistance.sources_to_windows_distance).

With coarsening, the windows of block centres \(c\), with interpolation weights \(T_c(i)\) and blocks of \(b\) pixels a side (see WindowedAnalysis), estimate the gradient.

Quality. With q_weighted and a symmetric distance (see AbstractDistance.symmetric), the derivative is \(2 \sum_{j \neq i} K_{ij} q_j\), interpolated from the block centres without differentiation:

\[\frac{\partial C}{\partial q_i} \approx 2 \sum_c T_c(i) \sum_{j \neq c} K_{cj} q_j\]

Otherwise, the result is the gradient of the coarsened connectivity.

Permeability. With a distance that averages sources (see AbstractDistance.averages_sources), such as ResistanceDistance, the result is the gradient of

\[\sum_c \Big(\sum_i T_c(i)\, q_i\Big) \sum_j \big(1 - u_c(j)\big)\, K\Big(\frac{\bar d_{cj}}{1 - u_c(j)}\Big)\, q_j, \qquad \bar d_{cj} = \sum_i u_c(i)\, d_{ij}, \qquad u_c(i) = \frac{T_c(i)\, q_i}{\sum_k T_c(k)\, q_k},\]

over the pixels \(j\) of the window of \(c\) with \(u_c(j) < 1\), where \(u_c\) is the block source of \(c\): the pixels that \(c\) stands for, weighted as in its sum. \(\bar d_{cj}\), the mean of their distances to \(j\), comes from one window query, and \(\bar d_{cj} / (1 - u_c(j))\) is the mean without \(j\) itself, as \(d_{jj} = 0\). For a proximity affine in the distance, the sum over \(j\) is \(\sum_i u_c(i) \sum_{j \neq i} K(d_{ij})\, q_j\): each pixel counts its pairs in the windows of its block centres.

With other distances, the gradient of \(\sum_c \big(\sum_i T_c(i)\, q_i\big) \sum_{j \notin \text{block}(c)} K_{cj} q_j\), without the pairs within blocks, is multiplied pixel by pixel by a block correction adapted from that of Omniscape:

\[\kappa(x) = \frac{\sum_c \sum_s w_c(s)\, g(x - c - s)} {\sum_c g_\text{far}(x - c) \sum_s w_c(s)}, \qquad w_c(s) = T_c(c + s).\]

The weights \(w_c(s)\) select the pixel windows that block centre \(c\) stands for. \(g\) and \(g_\text{far}\) are the permeability gradients of \(\sum_{j \neq c} K_{cj}\) and \(\sum_{j \notin \text{block}(c)} K_{cj}\) for one source at the centre of a window of quality 1 and of the raster's maximum permeability, computed once per run. \(g_\text{far}\) is set to 0 where its magnitude is at most 1e-6 times its largest, and \(\kappa = 1\) where the denominator is 0, as where proximities underflow.

Limitations

  • Coarsened sensitivities are approximate. The quality term falls steeply within dependency_range of the raster edges, where the interpolation underestimates it.
  • With block sources and a proximity convex in the distance, such as the default, the proximity of the mean distance is at most the mean of the proximities: the gap grows for pixels \(j\) near the block, and with the block size relative to the range of the proximity.
  • With distances that do not average sources, in a uniform landscape away from its edges, the corrected permeability gradient of a block window is the weighted sum of the gradients of its pixel windows, except in the band of up to \(b - 1\) pixels that they reach beyond it, whose gradients are lost. The block correction is biased near the raster edges, on tiles larger than windows, whose graphs extend beyond the windows, and around barriers, where it leaves marks along the lattice of block centres.
  • Randomized distances give noisy sensitivities to permeability where permeability varies over orders of magnitude: lower epsilon, or compare seeds.

Example

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape import ResistanceDistance, SensitivityAnalysis

sens = SensitivityAnalysis(
    quality_raster=quality,
    permeability_raster=permeability,
    distance=ResistanceDistance(),
    dependency_range=20,
    batch_size=100,
)

d_quality = sens.run("quality", q_weighted=True)
d_permeability = sens.run("permeability", q_weighted=True)

# Identify conservation priorities
high_impact = d_quality > jnp.percentile(d_quality, 90)

docs.title: run(var: str = 'quality', q_weighted: bool = True) -> Array
docs.text:
Compute the gradient of connectivity with respect to a raster.

Arguments:

  • var: Parameter to differentiate: "quality" or "permeability".
  • q_weighted: If True, differentiate the connectivity weighted by habitat quality. If False, differentiate the sum of proximities alone.

Returns:

Gradient raster with the shape of the input rasters: the sensitivity of connectivity at each pixel. Pixels whose permeability is at or below the permeability floor have a sensitivity to permeability of zero.

docs.title: Distances
docs.text: A distance object (AbstractDistance) takes a graph and returns the distances between some of its vertices. LCPDistance, ResistanceDistance and FreeEnergyDistance compute them from the edge weights, which they read as conductances; EuclideanDistance computes them from the pixel coordinates of a GridGraph. Every distance is called in the same way: distance(graph, nodes=nodes) for the distances among nodes, distance(graph, sources=sources, targets=targets) for the distances from sources to targets, and distance(graph) for the distances between all pairs of vertices. ResistanceDistance and FreeEnergyDistance solve linear systems, with a solver chosen as Linear solvers describes.

docs.title: Interface
docs.text: AbstractDistance defines the queries of every distance. AbstractSolverDistance adds the solver state of the distances that solve linear systems.

docs.title: jaxscape.distance.AbstractDistance
docs.text:
Abstract base class for distance computations on graphs.

A distance is called on a graph, with vertices given as vertex indices or, on a GridGraph, as pixel coordinates.

Arguments:

  • graph: Graph on which to compute distances.
  • sources: Source vertices, as vertex indices with shape (m,) or, for a GridGraph, pixel coordinates with shape (m, 2).
  • targets: Target vertices, as vertex indices with shape (k,) or, for a GridGraph, pixel coordinates with shape (k, 2).
  • nodes: Vertices of the pairwise distances, as vertex indices with shape (k,) or, for a GridGraph, pixel coordinates with shape (k, 2).
  • state: Optional solver state. Defaults to automatic initialization.

Specify either: nodes alone, sources and/or targets, or neither (for all-pairs).

Attributes:

  • sources_share_work: Whether a query from several sources costs much less than one query per source, as when the linear systems that a query solves serve every source with one solver state, such as a factorization or a multigrid hierarchy. Windowed analyses then compute the distances of many sources on the graph of one tile. Defaults to False.
  • symmetric: Whether the distance from i to j equals the distance from j to i on graphs whose adjacency matrix is symmetric, as those of windowed analyses are. With coarsening, SensitivityAnalysis then computes the sensitivity of the quality-weighted connectivity to quality without differentiation. Defaults to False.
  • averages_sources: Whether window queries take source_weights and return the mean of the distances from the pixels around each source, with these weights, at the cost of one query (see sources_to_windows_distance). With coarsening, SensitivityAnalysis then computes the sensitivity of connectivity to the permeability of a block centre from the distances of its block source, the pixels that the block centre stands for. Defaults to False.

Returns:

Distance array with shape depending on the inputs.

Example

from jaxscape import LCPDistance, GridGraph
import jax.numpy as jnp

distance = LCPDistance()
permeability = jnp.ones((12, 12))
grid = GridGraph(permeability, fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)

# All-pairs distance
D = distance(grid)  # Shape: (n_nodes, n_nodes)

# Using vertex indices
D = distance(
    grid,
    sources=jnp.array([0, 1]),
    targets=jnp.array([10, 20]),
)

# Using coordinates (for GridGraph)
D = distance(
    grid,
    sources=jnp.array([[0, 0], [1, 1]]),
    targets=jnp.array([[10, 10]]),
)

# Pairwise among subset
D = distance(grid, nodes=jnp.array([0, 5, 10]))  # Shape: (3, 3)

docs.title: reinit(graph: AbstractGraph, state: typing.Any) -> typing.Any
docs.text:
Return the state for graph, reusing what the solver can from state.

Queries on graph take the returned state, and so does the next reinit. Carry the returned state into the next queries and reinit, whatever the distance and solver. The state is None for a distance without a solver, such as one with solver=None. With Lineax's and JAXScape's solvers, it is never None. For a solver that keeps nothing from one matrix to the next, such as lineax.CG, reinit ignores state and returns init(graph).

Arguments:

  • graph: Graph of the next queries.
  • state: State from init or an earlier reinit.

Returns:

State for graph, without gradient.

docs.title: sources_to_windows_distance(graph: GridGraph, sources: Array, size: int, state: typing.Any = None, source_weights: jax.Array | None = None) -> Array
docs.text:
Return the distances from each source to the pixels of its window.

The window of a source is the square of size pixels a side centred on it, and it must lie inside the grid: the query raises otherwise. Windowed analyses query the distances of their block centres through this method, and the profile of their default proximity through a sources-to-targets query. By default, it computes the distances from the sources to every vertex and slices their windows: it holds m * n distances for m sources and n vertices, besides the memory of the query. A distance may override it to hold fewer values, as ResistanceDistance does, or for speed, as LCPDistance does on grid graphs.

Arguments:

  • graph: Grid graph on which to compute distances.
  • sources: Source vertex indices with shape (m,).
  • size: Odd number of pixels along a side of the windows.
  • state: Optional solver state. Defaults to automatic initialization.
  • source_weights: Optional weights of the pixels around each source, for distances that average sources (see averages_sources); other distances raise. Defaults to the source alone.

Returns:

Distances with shape (m, size, size). For source i at row r and column c, entry [i, a, b] is the distance to the pixel at row r - size // 2 + a and column c - size // 2 + b.

docs.title: exact() -> AbstractDistance
docs.text:
Return the distance whose values the queries of this one estimate.

Distances that queries compute exactly return themselves. Their solver states serve each other.

Returns:

The distance that this one estimates, or this one.

docs.title: debiased_proximity(proximity: collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array], graph: AbstractGraph) -> collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array]
docs.text:
Return the proximity to apply to the distances of queries on graph.

Applied to randomized distances, it has the expectation of proximity applied to exact distances. Distances that queries compute exactly return proximity.

Arguments:

  • proximity: Function mapping distances to proximities.
  • graph: Graph of the queries.

Returns:

Function mapping the distances of queries on graph to proximities.

docs.title: jaxscape.distance.AbstractSolverDistance
docs.text:
Distance whose queries solve linear systems in one sparse matrix per graph.

That matrix is the system matrix of the graph: sparse, symmetric and positive definite, such as the grounded Laplacian of ResistanceDistance. Subclass it with solver and system_matrix to get the solver state lifecycle of init and reinit.

Attributes:

  • solver: Lineax solver of linear systems in the system matrix, or None for dense linear algebra.

docs.title: system_matrix(graph: AbstractGraph) -> BCOO
docs.text:
Return the system matrix of graph.

Arguments:

  • graph: Graph of the queries.

Returns:

The system matrix, as a BCOO matrix.

docs.title: init(graph: AbstractGraph) -> typing.Any
docs.text:
Build the solver state for graph.

JAXScape's sparse solvers, except CholmodSolver, read concrete sparse indices, and AMJaxCGSolver builds its preconditioner on the host, so call it outside jax.jit. ResistanceDistance also builds the state of a GridGraph inside jax.jit.

init returns the state that solver.init builds for the system matrix: a state for Lineax's and JAXScape's solvers, and None only with solver=None. Carry the state through reinit and the queries whatever the solver. For a solver that keeps nothing from one matrix to the next, such as lineax.CG, reinit ignores state and returns init(graph).

Arguments:

  • graph: Graph whose system matrix the state is built for.

Returns:

State to pass to queries and to reinit, or None without a solver.

docs.title: Euclidean distance
docs.text: The straight-line distance between pixels, in pixels. It does not depend on the edge weights.

docs.title: jaxscape.euclidean_distance.EuclideanDistance
docs.text:
Straight-line distance between pixels, in pixels. It requires a GridGraph. Distances take the floating dtype of the grid, or JAX's default floating dtype for an integer or boolean grid.

Example

from jaxscape import EuclideanDistance

distance = EuclideanDistance()
dist = distance(grid, sources=source_coords, targets=target_coords)

docs.title: Least-cost path distance
docs.text: The smallest sum of the edge costs 1 / a along a path between two vertices, for the conductance a of each edge.

docs.title: jaxscape.lcp_distance.LCPDistance
docs.text:
Compute least-cost path distances with edge cost 1/a for conductance a, using algorithm.

For V vertices, E stored edges and S requested sources:

  • Bellman–Ford (default): Relaxes sparse edges until distances stop changing. Each round costs O(S(V + E)), and it takes one round more than the most edges on a shortest path, at most V − 1. Favor it for sparse graphs or a small number of sources. Window queries on a GridGraph relax the grid by shifting rasters (see sources_to_windows_distance).
  • Floyd–Warshall: Computes a dense all-pairs distance matrix by considering each vertex as an intermediate stop. Costs O(V³) time, even when requesting only selected pairs. Favor it for small dense graphs when most or all pairs are needed.

For a unique shortest path, the derivative of its distance with respect to a is -1/a**2 on that path and zero elsewhere: increasing conductance decreases the distance. At exact ties, Bellman–Ford chooses a generalized gradient by splitting sensitivity equally among optimal incoming edges at each vertex; complete paths need not receive equal weight. Raster gradients follow by the chain rule through GridGraph.fun.

Attributes:

  • algorithm: "bellman-ford" (default) or "floyd-warshall".

Note

Bellman–Ford requires positive, finite conductances; zero means no edge. Gradients assume that the edges of the graph stay the same. jax.jvp, jax.jacfwd, and higher-order derivatives are currently unsupported.

Example

from jaxscape import LCPDistance, GridGraph
import jax.numpy as jnp

grid = GridGraph(jnp.ones((5, 5)), fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)
distance = LCPDistance()
D = distance(grid, sources=jnp.array([0, 1]), targets=jnp.array([10, 20]))

docs.title: sources_to_windows_distance(graph: GridGraph, sources: Array, size: int, state: typing.Any = None, source_weights: jax.Array | None = None) -> Array
docs.text:
Return the distances from each source to the pixels of its window.

As AbstractDistance.sources_to_windows_distance. With Bellman–Ford, a relaxation round shifts the distance rasters of all sources by each neighbour offset of graph, adds the edge costs and takes elementwise minima: a few fused operations, without the gathers and scatters of sparse edges, which are slow on GPUs. With four neighbours, one expression runs two rounds. The adjoint propagation of the gradient shifts rasters the same way. The distances are those of the sparse edges, exactly, and the gradients the same to rounding. Windowed analyses run faster this way than with sparse edges, on GPUs and on CPUs.

Rounds cannot be fewer: each distance is the sum of the edge costs of a shortest path, rounded after each edge, which the backward pass relies on to find the edges of shortest paths. Sweeps along rows and columns as prefix scans would add costs in another order.

The query needs concrete graph.neighbors; when they are traced, as for a graph passed into jax.jit, it relaxes the sparse edges.

Arguments:

  • graph: Grid graph on which to compute distances.
  • sources: Source vertex indices with shape (m,).
  • size: Odd number of pixels along a side of the windows.
  • state: Ignored.
  • source_weights: Raises if given: least-cost path distances do not average sources.

Returns:

Distances with shape (m, size, size).

docs.title: Resistance distance
docs.text: The effective resistance between two vertices when each edge is a resistor of conductance a. Its method is ExactResistance, which computes it exactly, or SpielmanApproximation, which estimates it from random projections.

docs.title: jaxscape.resistance_distance.ResistanceDistance
docs.text:
Resistance distance: the effective resistance between two vertices of a graph whose edge weights are conductances.

Queries compute it by solving linear systems in the Laplacian of the graph grounded at one vertex, or from the pseudo-inverse of the Laplacian.

Attributes:

  • solver: Lineax solver of linear systems in the grounded Laplacian, for BCOO sparse matrices, or None for dense linear algebra. Defaults to jaxscape.solvers.GeometricMultigridCGSolver(), conjugate gradients with a geometric multigrid preconditioner, which solves the grounded Laplacians of grid graphs, such as those of a GridGraph, on any device without an optional dependency, also in float32 and inside jax.jit. With the default, queries on other graphs raise an error: pass jaxscape.solvers.CholmodSolver, AMJaxCGSolver or CuDSSSolver, or solver=None. Choosing a solver gives the solver for each device and query. Without a solver, exact all-pairs and nodes-to-nodes queries compute the pseudo-inverse of the dense Laplacian, and other queries a dense Cholesky factorization of the grounded Laplacian: their memory grows with the square of the number of vertices, which suits small graphs. Windowed analyses with exact resistances, which solve a linear system for every vertex of a tile, can run faster on a CPU without a solver. In float32, the pseudo-inverse loses accuracy when conductances span orders of magnitude.
  • method: A resistance distance method. Defaults to ExactResistance(). Use SpielmanApproximation(epsilon=..., seed=...) for the randomized Spielman-Srivastava approximation.

Example

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape import GridGraph, ResistanceDistance, SpielmanApproximation
from jaxscape.solvers import AMJaxCGSolver, CholmodSolver

permeability = jnp.ones((3, 3))
grid = GridGraph(permeability, fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)

# Default: GeometricMultigridCGSolver, for grid graphs
distance = ResistanceDistance()
dist = distance(grid)

# Dense solves, for small graphs of any kind
distance = ResistanceDistance(solver=None)

# A sparse direct solver, for other graphs
distance = ResistanceDistance(solver=CholmodSolver())

# With an initialized AMG-preconditioned CG solver
distance = ResistanceDistance(solver=AMJaxCGSolver(rtol=1e-6))
state = distance.init(grid)

dist = distance(grid, state=state)

# Carry a state from one graph to the next, as an optimization loop does.
# AMJax keeps its hierarchy.
updated_permeability = permeability * 1.1
updated_grid = GridGraph(updated_permeability, fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)
state = distance.reinit(updated_grid, state)
dist = distance(updated_grid, state=state)

# Approximate resistance distance, with the default solver
distance = ResistanceDistance(method=SpielmanApproximation(epsilon=0.05))

dist = distance(grid)

Grounding, float32 and memory

Except dense all-pairs and nodes-to-nodes queries, which compute the pseudo-inverse, queries solve linear systems in the Laplacian grounded at one vertex: among the vertices whose weighted degree is at least half the largest, the nearest to the middle vertex. On a grid graph of h rows and w columns, with rook or queen contiguity, the middle vertex is its centre pixel, of row h // 2 and column w // 2. The ground of a window or a tile of a windowed analysis is thus a pixel of high permeability at or near its centre, where its sources lie, which keeps float32 distances free of cancellation. A ground on a barrier would make the float32 system too ill-conditioned to solve.

On large tiles, the float32 solutions of sparse direct solvers are inaccurate around the ground vertex. For the sensitivity of connectivity to permeability on large tiles, use GeometricMultigridCGSolver, the default, in float32, or a direct solver in float64.

Exact sources-to-targets queries on n vertices, from m sources to k targets, hold the potentials of all targets when they are a few million values, as in small windows. Beyond, they solve the targets in chunks of c, about a thousand, and hold at most n * (m + c) potentials. Computing their gradient solves the system of each target once more.

Warning

The graph must be undirected for resistance distance to be well-defined. With a solver, it must also be connected: the grounded Laplacian of a disconnected graph is singular, and queries raise an error. GeometricMultigridCGSolver then reports a non-finite solution, or a solve that did not converge within max_steps. A grid graph is disconnected when edges of zero conductance cut it, as fun gives between pixels of zero permeability. Windowed analyses raise permeability to a floor, so that their graphs are connected. Without a solver, the pseudo-inverse gives the resistances within each connected component, and finite values between components, and sources-to-targets queries give NaN.

docs.title: sources_to_windows_distance(graph: GridGraph, sources: Array, size: int, state: typing.Any = None, source_weights: jax.Array | None = None) -> Array
docs.text:
Return the distances from each source to the pixels of its window.

As AbstractDistance.sources_to_windows_distance. With source_weights \(u\) of a source, its distance to pixel \(j\) is the mean of the resistances \(R_{ij}\) from the pixels \(i\) around it, with the weights \(u_i\):

\[\sum_i u_i R_{ij} = R_{uj} + \sum_i u_i R_{ui}, \qquad R_{uj} = (u - e_j)^T L^+ (u - e_j),\]

where \(L^+\) is the pseudo-inverse of the Laplacian, and \(R_{uj}\) the resistance between pixel \(j\) and the pixels of \(u\), which a unit current enters with the weights \(u\). The query computes \(R_{uj}\) for the pixels of the window, and adds the within-block mean resistance \(\sum_i u_i R_{ui}\), which is 0 for a source alone. Exact queries solve for the vector \(u\) in place of the source, and for every pixel of the graph.

With SpielmanApproximation, the query solves the k projections projection_batch_size at a time, and adds the squared differences of their potentials between each source, the mean of its pixels with the weights \(u\), and the pixels of its window. It holds the potentials of one batch of projections and the windows.

Its gradient estimates the gradient of the exact resistances, contracted with the cotangent of the estimates, from k random probes of the pairs of a source and a pixel of its window, solved projection_batch_size at a time with two right-hand sides each. Each probe draws a sign per source and a sign per pixel, whose product weighs a pair. The estimate of each stored edge is unbiased, and varies much less between seeds than the gradient of the estimates themselves. Its noise falls as epsilon decreases.

Arguments:

  • graph: Grid graph on which to compute distances.
  • sources: Source vertex indices with shape (m,).
  • size: Odd number of pixels along a side of the windows.
  • state: Optional solver state. Defaults to automatic initialization.
  • source_weights: Optional non-negative weights of the pixels around each source, centred on it, which sum to 1, with shape (m, side, side) for an odd side of at most size. Defaults to the source alone, side = 1.

Returns:

Distances with shape (m, size, size).

ResistanceDistance with ExactResistance and the solver of this one, whose solver states serve each other.

docs.title: debiased_proximity(proximity: collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array], graph: AbstractGraph) -> collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array]
docs.text:
Return the proximity to apply to the distances of queries on graph.

With SpielmanApproximation, an estimate \(\hat R\) of the resistance \(R\) is unbiased, with variance \(2 R^2 / k\) for \(k\) projections. A proximity \(K\) convex in \(R\) is then biased upward, by about \(R^2 K''(R) / k\), which grows with epsilon. The returned proximity is corrected to second order:

\[K(\hat R) - \frac{\hat R^2}{k} K''(\hat R)\]

For a negative exponential, it is \(K(\hat R) \big(1 - (\hat R K'(\hat R) / K(\hat R))^2 / k\big)\). The correction does not reduce the variance of the proximities. It assumes the variance of one pair: the mean resistances from source weights (see sources_to_windows_distance) vary less, and the correction of a convex proximity of them is slightly too large. Exact resistances keep proximity.

Arguments:

  • proximity: Function mapping resistances to proximities, twice differentiable.
  • graph: Graph of the queries.

Returns:

Function mapping the resistances of queries on graph to proximities.

docs.title: jaxscape.resistance_distance.ExactResistance
docs.text: Exact resistance distances, from the pseudo-inverse of the Laplacian or from linear systems in the grounded Laplacian.

docs.title: jaxscape.resistance_distance.SpielmanApproximation
docs.text:
Randomized approximation of resistance distances by the random projections of Spielman and Srivastava.

Attributes:

  • epsilon: Accuracy parameter. Smaller values use more random projections: k = ceil(log(n_vertices) / epsilon**2). All-pairs and sources-to-targets queries solve k linear systems and hold k potentials of every vertex; nodes-to-nodes queries solve one per node. Window queries, those of windowed analyses, solve k linear systems and hold the potentials of projection_batch_size of them. Their gradient solves 2 * k more, two right-hand sides for each of k random probes, projection_batch_size probes at a time.
  • seed: Random seed for the Rademacher edge projections. Each projection draws its signs from seed and its index, so that all queries on a graph share their projections, in float32 and float64, with and without 64-bit types (jax_enable_x64). The probes of the gradient of window queries draw their signs from the same seed.
  • projection_batch_size: Number of projections that window queries solve together. Other queries draw the random signs of this many projections together when the signs of all projections, one per stored edge and projection, exceed SPIELMAN_DENSE_PROJECTION_MAX_SIGN_ENTRIES entries, and all at once below. Larger batches can improve throughput at the cost of more working memory.

docs.title: Free-energy distance
docs.text: A distance set by the inverse temperature theta, between the least-cost path distance and the resistance distance: it approaches the least-cost path distance as theta grows, and a multiple of the resistance distance as theta tends to 0.

docs.title: jaxscape.free_energy_distance.FreeEnergyDistance
docs.text:
Symmetric first-hitting free-energy distance with edge costs \(1/a_{ij}\).

Attributes:

  • theta: Finite positive scalar inverse temperature. Larger values concentrate the path distribution on least-cost paths. Distances are differentiable with respect to theta.
  • solver: Lineax solver of linear systems in the system matrix, from the same choices as for ResistanceDistance, or None, the default, for dense linear algebra, which suits small graphs. Larger graphs need a sparse direct solver, CholmodSolver on CPU and CuDSSSolver on GPU: iterative solvers, GeometricMultigridCGSolver included, need tolerances far below their defaults to resolve the small entries of \(Z\) between distant vertices. See Choosing a solver.

For conductances \(a_{ij}\), let \(c_{ij}=1/a_{ij}\) on present edges, \(P_{ij}=a_{ij}/\sum_k a_{ik}\), and \(Z=(I-P\odot e^{-\theta C})^{-1}\). The first-hitting partition is \(z^h_{ij}=Z_{ij}/Z_{jj}\) and \(d_{ij}=-(\log z^h_{ij}+\log z^h_{ji})/(2\theta)\). For the derivation, see Kivimäki, Shimbo & Saerens and Françoisse et al..

The graph must be connected and symmetric, with positive finite conductances on present edges. Conductance enters both the edge costs and the transition probabilities. As theta grows, the distance approaches the least-cost path distance with edge costs \(c_{ij}\). On a graph without self-loops and with m undirected edges, the small-theta limit is m times the effective resistance. Solver state depends on the conductances and on theta; pass it through reinit when either changes.

Precision and errors: float32 and float64 inputs are supported. Entries of \(Z\) decay exponentially with path cost, and float64 resolves smaller entries, hence larger distances and larger theta. The logarithm of each queried entry is checked against an error estimate computed from the residual of the solve; entries that the precision does not resolve raise an EquinoxRuntimeError, and are never clipped or substituted. The estimate includes heuristic rounding allowances, so accuracy should be validated for the intended workload. Checks use eqx.error_if; on GPU, a failed check may be reported without raising, depending on EQX_ON_ERROR.

Differentiation: first-order reverse-mode differentiation reuses the solutions of the forward computation. Forward-mode and higher-order derivatives are not validated.

Example

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape import FreeEnergyDistance, GridGraph

raster = jnp.array([[0.8, 1.2], [1.4, 0.9]])
grid = GridGraph(raster, fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)
distances = FreeEnergyDistance(theta=0.5)(grid, nodes=jnp.array([0, 3]))

docs.title: Graphs
docs.text: Distances are computed on a graph, from its edge weights read as conductances. GridGraph builds the graph of a raster: one vertex per pixel, and edges between neighbouring pixels, whose weights fun computes from the pixel values. The grid graphs of one raster shape and contiguity can share a GridTopology, which holds their edges. Graph holds any graph, given by its weighted adjacency matrix.

docs.text: Abstract base class for graphs.

docs.text: Get the adjacency matrix of the graph.

docs.text:
Graph given by its weighted adjacency matrix.

Arguments:

  • adjacency_matrix: Adjacency matrix, as a jax.experimental.sparse.BCOO matrix of shape (n, n) for n vertices. Entry (i, j) is the weight of the edge from vertex i to vertex j, which distances read as a conductance.

docs.title: jaxscape.graph.GridGraph
docs.text:
Graph whose vertices are the pixels of a raster, with edges between neighbouring pixels.

The pixel of row i and column j is the vertex i * width + j.

Arguments:

  • grid: Raster of pixel values, such as permeability, with shape (height, width), from which fun computes the edge weights. Distances read the edge weights as conductances, the inverses of resistances: higher values ease movement.
  • fun: Function of the values of the source and target pixels of the edges that returns their weights. It takes two arrays and returns an array of the same shape. Defaults to the value of the target pixel, fun = lambda x, y: y.
  • neighbors: Contiguity pattern, either ROOK_CONTIGUITY or QUEEN_CONTIGUITY. Defaults to ROOK_CONTIGUITY, or to the contiguity of topology; pass one or the other.
  • topology: Optional GridTopology of the shape of grid, built once for the graphs of one raster shape and contiguity, as in a loop over conductance surfaces. The adjacency matrix then reads its edges and computes the edge weights alone; it is the same with and without a topology.
