docs.title: jaxscape.graph.GridTopology
docs.text:
The edges of the grid graphs of one raster shape and contiguity.

It holds what their adjacency matrices share whatever the conductances: the source and target of each edge, which set the sparsity pattern of the matrices. In graph terms, it is their underlying, unweighted graph.

A GridGraph alone rebuilds these edges each time it builds its adjacency matrix, although only the weights change from one conductance surface to the next, as when an optimizer fits a surface. A topology builds them once: pass it to each GridGraph of that shape and contiguity, and the graph computes its edge weights alone. Its adjacency matrix equals that of the same GridGraph without topology. Build the topology outside jax.jit and pass it in, so that compiled programs read its edges.

Arguments:

  • shape: Raster shape (height, width).
  • neighbors: Contiguity pattern, either ROOK_CONTIGUITY or QUEEN_CONTIGUITY, or another array of (row, column) offsets with shape (k, 2). It must be concrete, outside of a trace.

Example

import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape import GridGraph, GridTopology, ResistanceDistance

def fun(x, y):
    return (x + y) / 2

topology = GridTopology((50, 50))
surfaces = jnp.exp(jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (4, 50, 50)))
sites = jnp.array([0, 1275, 2499])

distance = ResistanceDistance()
state = distance.init(GridGraph(surfaces[0], fun=fun, topology=topology))

@eqx.filter_jit
def resistances(surface, topology, state):
    graph = GridGraph(surface, fun=fun, topology=topology)
    state = distance.reinit(graph, state)
    return distance.nodes_to_nodes_distance(graph, sites, state), state

for surface in surfaces:
    resistance, state = resistances(surface, topology, state)

docs.title: Linear solvers
docs.text: Computing resistance and free-energy distances, and their gradients, requires solving linear systems in a sparse symmetric positive definite matrix of the graph, which AbstractSolverDistance.system_matrix returns. For ResistanceDistance, this matrix is the graph Laplacian grounded at one vertex. For FreeEnergyDistance, with conductances \(a_{ij}\) and inverse temperature \(\theta\), it is the Laplacian of the edge weights \(a_{ij} e^{-\theta / a_{ij}}\) plus the positive diagonal \(\kappa_i = \sum_j a_{ij} (1 - e^{-\theta / a_{ij}})\). A linear solver, passed as the solver argument of the distance, solves these systems; with solver=None, the distances are computed with dense linear algebra instead. The solver sets the runtime, the memory and the accuracy of the distances.

docs.title: Choosing a solver
docs.text:
The default solver of ResistanceDistance is GeometricMultigridCGSolver(): conjugate gradients (CG) preconditioned by geometric multigrid, in JAX on CPU and GPU, for the matrices of grid graphs such as those of GridGraph. On other graphs, the default solver raises an error; pass solver. FreeEnergyDistance uses dense linear algebra by default, solver=None.

Distance and query GPU CPU Resistance distances among a few vertices: nodes_to_nodes_distance, few sources and targets, gradient-based fitting of conductances to observed distances, and SpielmanApproximation GeometricMultigridCGSolver, the default GeometricMultigridCGSolver, the default Resistance distances from one or all sources to every vertex: all_pairs_distance, and windowed analyses with ExactResistance solver=None for small graphs and tiles; GeometricMultigridCGSolver for larger ones solver=None for small graphs and tiles; CholmodSolver for larger ones Free-energy distances solver=None, the default, for small graphs; CuDSSSolver for larger ones solver=None for small graphs; CholmodSolver for larger ones Resistance or free-energy distances on graphs other than grid graphs solver=None for small graphs; CuDSSSolver for larger ones; AMJaxCGSolver when the factorization does not fit in memory solver=None for small graphs; CholmodSolver for larger ones; AMJaxCGSolver when the factorization does not fit in memory

In float64, on GPUs of low float64 throughput, CuDSSSolver can compute resistance distances faster than GeometricMultigridCGSolver.

Memory restricts the choice first. Dense linear algebra stores matrices of \(n^2\) entries for a graph of \(n\) vertices, and so fits small graphs only. GeometricMultigridCGSolver stores the matrix on its grid and a few arrays of \(n\) entries per right-hand side. Sparse direct solvers store a factorization of the matrix; when it does not fit in memory, use GeometricMultigridCGSolver on grid graphs and AMJaxCGSolver on other graphs.

The entries of the inverse of the free-energy system matrix decay exponentially with path cost. Iterative solvers therefore need tolerances far below their defaults to resolve the distances between distant vertices, and in float32, the distances are accurate over a limited range of theta on a given landscape.

With a solver, ResistanceDistance requires a connected graph: the grounded Laplacian of a disconnected graph is singular, and queries raise an error. A grid graph is disconnected when some of its pixels are joined to the others only by edges of zero conductance, such as the edges that the weight function fun of GridGraph gives between pixels of zero permeability. Windowed analyses raise permeability to a floor value, so that their graphs are connected.

The tolerance at which a solver gives accurate distances depends on the query and on the floating-point precision. A solver can converge and still give inaccurate distances: check the distances of your queries, for example against solver=None on a small graph. The measurements behind this page are in issue #35.

docs.title: Lineax solvers
docs.text:
Any Lineax solver of sparse symmetric positive definite operators can be passed as solver, such as conjugate gradients without preconditioner, lineax.CG:

import lineax as lx
from jaxscape import FreeEnergyDistance, ResistanceDistance

solver = lx.CG(rtol=1e-6, atol=1e-6)
resistance = ResistanceDistance(solver=solver)
free_energy = FreeEnergyDistance(theta=0.2, solver=solver)

The distance passes its system matrix to the solver as a BCOOLinearOperator. The Lineax documentation lists the available solvers and their options.

docs.title: JAXScape solvers
docs.text:
jaxscape.solvers provides four solvers. GeometricMultigridCGSolver needs no optional dependency. Each of the three others needs one, installed with an extra of jaxscape:

uv add jaxscape --extra cholespy   # CholmodSolver
uv add jaxscape --extra amjax      # AMJaxCGSolver
uv add jaxscape --extra cudss      # CuDSSSolver (NVIDIA GPU, CUDA 13)
Solver Method Execution Graphs GeometricMultigridCGSolver Conjugate gradients preconditioned by geometric multigrid JAX, on CPU or GPU Grid graphs AMJaxCGSolver Conjugate gradients preconditioned by algebraic multigrid Preconditioner built on the CPU; solves in JAX, on CPU or GPU Any connected graph CholmodSolver Sparse Cholesky factorization CHOLMOD on the CPU, through a host callback Any connected graph CuDSSSolver Sparse Cholesky factorization NVIDIA cuDSS on the GPU, inside jax.jit Any connected graph

A host callback runs Python code on the CPU from a compiled JAX program. Arrays on a GPU then travel to the CPU and back.

docs.title: Geometric multigrid
docs.text:
GeometricMultigridCGSolver solves the matrices of grid graphs, such as the grounded Laplacian of a GridGraph with rook or queen contiguity, by conjugate gradients preconditioned by geometric multigrid. It is the default solver of ResistanceDistance. It runs in JAX on CPU and GPU, in float32 and float64, inside jax.jit, and needs no optional dependency.

Theory: multigrid preconditioning

The number of conjugate gradient iterations grows with the condition number of the matrix, which grows with the size of the grid and with the contrast of conductances. A preconditioner is an approximate inverse of the matrix, which the solver applies at each iteration, so that it reaches the tolerance in fewer iterations. In multigrid, the solver builds the preconditioner from a hierarchy of coarser grids: by relaxation on a grid, it lowers the components of the error that vary from pixel to pixel, and by corrections on the coarser grids, the components that vary smoothly, at a fraction of the cost. In geometric multigrid, the solver builds the coarser grids from the raster: each holds every other pixel along each axis. The cycle, the interpolation between grids and the solve on the coarsest grid are given in the API entry of GeometricMultigridCGSolver below.

The preconditioner of its state is the grid, a raster shape and contiguity. init reads the grid from the sparse indices of the matrix; distance.init(graph) reads it from the shape and contiguity of a GridGraph, also inside jax.jit. reinit replaces the values of the matrix with those of another matrix of the same grid. Each solve builds the multigrid hierarchy of the matrix it solves, so that each tile of a windowed analysis is solved with the hierarchy of its own conductances.

from jaxscape import ResistanceDistance, SpielmanApproximation
from jaxscape.solvers import GeometricMultigridCGSolver

exact = ResistanceDistance()  # GeometricMultigridCGSolver(rtol=1e-5)
approximate = ResistanceDistance(
    solver=GeometricMultigridCGSolver(rtol=3e-4),
    method=SpielmanApproximation(epsilon=0.15),
)

rtol is the bound on the norm of the residual that conjugate gradients update at each iteration, relative to the norm of the right-hand side. With a larger rtol, the solves take fewer iterations. In float32, because of rounding, the residual b - A x of the solution x stops decreasing at some level; with an rtol below that level, the iterations continue without improving the solution. The resistances to pixels behind barriers converge last: with a large rtol, the gradient of the distances with respect to the permeability of these pixels loses accuracy first.

In float32 on grid graphs, GeometricMultigridCGSolver gives the most accurate resistance distances of the JAXScape solvers. In float32, sparse direct solvers give inaccurate solutions around the ground vertex of large tiles (see the note on grounding of ResistanceDistance): use them in float64.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.geometricmultigridcgsolver.GeometricMultigridCGSolver
docs.text:
Conjugate gradients preconditioned by geometric multigrid, for grid graphs.

Solves the symmetric positive definite matrices whose sparsity pattern is a grid stencil, such as the grounded Laplacians of a GridGraph with rook or queen contiguity, in which ResistanceDistance solves linear systems. It is the default solver of ResistanceDistance. It runs in JAX, on any device, in float32 and float64, and needs no optional dependency. Its preconditioner is the grid, which init reads from concrete sparse indices. Each solve builds the multigrid hierarchy of the current values on it, at a small fraction of the cost of the solve. A compiled program then holds one hierarchy for each place where it solves, whatever the states it reinitializes.

Each V-cycle has one iteration of damped Jacobi relaxation before and after the coarse correction. The coarse grids hold every other point along each axis. The values at the other points are interpolated from the matrix coefficients, as in black-box multigrid (Dendy, 1982), so that convergence stays fast across jumps of conductance. The matrices of the coarse grids are the Galerkin products of the interpolation. The first grid of at most 1024 points is solved with a Cholesky factorization.

With a larger rtol, the solves take fewer iterations, at the cost of the accuracy of the resistances to pixels behind barriers, which converge last. On large grids in float32, the solutions of this solver stay accurate around the ground vertex of ResistanceDistance, where those of sparse direct solvers lose accuracy. It factorizes only the matrix of the coarsest grid, which suits conductances that change at every step, as in optimization loops. In float64, sparse direct solvers can be faster.

Attributes:

  • rtol: Largest Euclidean norm of the residual, relative to that of the right-hand side (see AbstractSparseIterativeSolver).
  • max_steps: Largest number of iterations.

Warning

A state belongs to one grid: a raster shape and contiguity, with any conductances. The matrix must be positive definite: a grounded Laplacian of a connected graph. The solves of a singular matrix fail with lineax.RESULTS.singular when their solution is not finite, and with lineax.RESULTS.max_steps_reached otherwise.

docs.title: Algebraic multigrid
docs.text:
In algebraic multigrid, the coarser levels are built from the entries of the matrix, without a grid, so that the matrix of any graph can be preconditioned. AMJaxCGSolver solves by conjugate gradients preconditioned by an algebraic multigrid hierarchy, built by smoothed aggregation by default. It suits graphs other than grid graphs whose sparse Cholesky factorization does not fit in memory.

AMJaxCGSolver builds the hierarchy once, in init, on the CPU. It solves by conjugate gradients, preconditioned by V-cycles of the hierarchy, in JAX on CPU or GPU, inside jax.jit and jax.grad. reinit keeps the prolongation and restriction operators of the hierarchy, and each solve computes the matrices of its coarser levels from the current values, as Galerkin products with these operators. The state also holds, for each level but the coarsest, the map from the values of the level to those of the next: sparse matrices several times the size of the hierarchy. The hierarchy has the dtype of the matrix. For ill-conditioned graph Laplacians, enable 64-bit floats with JAX_ENABLE_X64=true and build the matrix and the right-hand sides in float64: enabling 64-bit floats does not convert existing float32 arrays. A matrix whose hierarchy has a single level, as that of a small graph, is solved by conjugate gradients without preconditioner.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.amjaxcgsolver.AMJaxCGSolver
docs.text:
Conjugate gradients preconditioned by algebraic multigrid, with AMJax.

Its preconditioner is a multigrid hierarchy, which init builds once on the host with PyAMG, from the values it is given, and converts to an AMJax hierarchy. Each solve applies one V-cycle of that hierarchy per iteration, in JAX, inside jax.jit and jax.grad. reinit keeps the prolongation and restriction operators of the hierarchy, and each solve computes the matrices of its coarser levels from the current values, as Galerkin products with these operators. The state also holds, for each level but the coarsest, the map from the values of the level to those of the next: sparse matrices several times the size of the hierarchy. The hierarchy keeps the dtype of the matrix. With a hierarchy of a single level, as that of a tiny graph, conjugate gradients run without a preconditioner.

Example

from jaxscape import ResistanceDistance
from jaxscape.solvers import AMJaxCGSolver

distance = ResistanceDistance(solver=AMJaxCGSolver(rtol=1e-6))
state = distance.init(grid)  # builds the hierarchy
dist = distance(grid, state=state)

Attributes:

  • rtol: Largest Euclidean norm of the residual, relative to that of the right-hand side (see AbstractSparseIterativeSolver).
  • max_steps: Largest number of iterations.
  • pyamg_method: The PyAMG function that builds the hierarchy from a SciPy CSR matrix. Defaults to pyamg.smoothed_aggregation_solver.
  • pyamg_kwargs: Keyword arguments of pyamg_method.
  • presmoother, postsmoother: AMJax smoothers, as (name, kwargs), both required. Default to one iteration of Jacobi of weight 2/3. A Jacobi smoother with withrho=True keeps the weight that init computes from the spectral radius of its level.
  • coarse_solver: AMJax solver of the coarsest level. The coarse solvers "pinv", "lu" and "qr" keep the factorization of the coarsest matrix of init.
  • coarse_solver_kwargs: Keyword arguments of coarse_solver.

Warning

amjax and pyamg must be installed to use this solver, with uv add jaxscape --extra amjax. Conjugate gradients need a symmetric positive definite V-cycle. With Jacobi smoothers of weight ω and the "jacobi" coarse solver, the V-cycle is one when ω times the spectral radius of D⁻¹A, for the matrix A of a level and its diagonal D, is below 2 on every level; on the coarsest level, ω is the weight of the coarse solver, 1 by default. With values other than those of init, a coarser level can have a spectral radius above 2, and the default weight of the smoothers, 2/3, admits spectral radii up to 3 on the levels they smooth.

docs.title: Sparse direct solvers
docs.text:
A sparse Cholesky factorization of the matrix is a product \(L L^\top\), with \(L\) sparse and lower triangular, after a reordering of its rows and columns that limits the number of entries of \(L\). Each solve then takes two triangular solves. The factorization costs far more than a solve, and many right-hand sides share it. Its cost depends on the sparsity pattern of the matrix only, and is the same whatever the contrast of conductances. CholmodSolver and CuDSSSolver solve the matrix of any connected graph. In float32, their solutions on large grids are inaccurate around the ground vertex of ResistanceDistance.

CholmodSolver factorizes with CHOLMOD, through cholespy, on the CPU, through a host callback. Solves reuse the last factorization while the values of the matrix stay the same.

CuDSSSolver factorizes with NVIDIA cuDSS, through spineax, on the GPU, inside jax.jit. Its state keeps the analysis of the sparsity pattern: the ordering of the rows and columns and the structure of \(L\). A matrix with new values is factorized on this analysis. It needs an NVIDIA GPU and Linux x86-64.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.cholmodsolver.CholmodSolver
docs.text:
Sparse Cholesky factorization with CHOLMOD, through cholespy, on the CPU.

Solves symmetric positive definite matrices through a host callback. Solves reuse the last factorization while the values of the matrix stay the same, and factorize the matrix again when they change. The solver keeps one factorization, so under jax.vmap over the values of the matrix, each solve factorizes every distinct matrix of the batch.

Attributes:

  • factorize_in_init: Whether init, called outside jax.jit, factorizes the matrix. Otherwise, or when init runs inside jax.jit, the first solve factorizes it. Defaults to True.

Example

from jaxscape.solvers import CholmodSolver

solver = CholmodSolver()
distance = ResistanceDistance(solver=solver)
state = distance.init(grid)  # factorizes the grounded Laplacian
dist = distance(grid, state=state)

Warning

cholespy must be installed to use this solver, with uv add jaxscape --extra cholespy.

Warning

Float64 solves run through a host callback, and require 64-bit floats enabled for the whole process before JAX computes anything, with JAX_ENABLE_X64=1 or jax.config.update("jax_enable_x64", True). A with jax.enable_x64() block enables them in its own thread only, and the host callback then fails with a dtype mismatch such as Expected: float64, Actual: float32.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.cudsssolver.CuDSSSolver
docs.text:
Sparse Cholesky solver running NVIDIA cuDSS on the GPU through spineax.

Solves float32 and float64 systems. A query solves all its right-hand sides in one call of cuDSS, with one factorization. JAX does not differentiate through the solves: the gradients are computed from the solutions or the factorization of the query. See AbstractSparseDirectSolver for the checks of each factorization and solve.

Warning

It needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA-enabled JAX, and raises an error naming what is missing elsewhere. The cudss extra, uv add jaxscape --extra cudss, installs spineax and cuDSS for CUDA 13, on Linux x86-64. It brings JAX's CUDA 13 plugin, so leave out the cuda extra. For CUDA 12, build spineax from source as in these notes.

Warning

The factorizations are held outside JAX's memory pool, so leave room with XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_PREALLOCATE=false. SPINEAX_FACTOR_CACHE sets the number of factorizations that spineax keeps in device memory.

Note

reinit consumes the factorization of the state it refactorizes. A used-up state, or one evicted from spineax's cache, still gives correct solutions, but each solve with it repeats the analysis, which is costly: pass each new state to the next reinit. In float32, on large grids, a matrix with vertices cut off from the ground vertex can pass the solve check; use float64 when conductances can be zero.

Note

In float32, solutions on large grids are inaccurate around the ground vertex of ResistanceDistance. For permeability sensitivity on large tiles, use float64, or GeometricMultigridCGSolver in float32.

docs.title: Reusing solver state
docs.text:
Building the state of a solver, as a sparse factorization or a multigrid hierarchy, can cost far more than a solve. ResistanceDistance and FreeEnergyDistance share one state lifecycle:

  • distance.init(graph) builds the state for the system matrix of graph. JAXScape's sparse solvers, except CholmodSolver, read concrete sparse indices, and AMJaxCGSolver runs code on the CPU, so call it outside jax.jit. ResistanceDistance also builds the state of a GridGraph inside jax.jit, from the shape and contiguity of the graph. The compiled program then holds the arrays of the state as constants: on large grids, it compiles faster with the state passed as an argument.
  • distance.reinit(graph, state) returns the state for another graph of the same sparsity pattern, and keeps what the solver can reuse. It runs inside jax.jit.
  • Queries take the state as state, and the queries on one graph can share it. A query always solves the system matrix of the graph it receives: an outdated state can make the query slower, and leaves its distances unchanged.

An optimization loop over conductances passes the state from one step to the next, whatever the solver. distance.init returns a state with Lineax's and JAXScape's solvers, and None only with solver=None. For a solver that keeps nothing from one matrix to the next, such as lineax.CG, reinit ignores the state and returns init(graph). The state has no gradient: with has_aux=True, the differentiated function returns it alongside the loss.

import equinox as eqx
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape import GridGraph, ResistanceDistance


def landscape(log_conductance):
    return GridGraph(jnp.exp(log_conductance), fun=lambda x, y: (x + y) / 2)


sites = jnp.array([0, 45, 99])
true_log_conductance = jax.random.normal(jax.random.key(0), (10, 10))
target = ResistanceDistance()(landscape(true_log_conductance), nodes=sites)

distance = ResistanceDistance()  # GeometricMultigridCGSolver
log_conductance = jnp.zeros((10, 10))
state = distance.init(landscape(log_conductance))


def loss(log_conductance, state):
    grid = landscape(log_conductance)
    state = distance.reinit(grid, state)
    predicted = distance.nodes_to_nodes_distance(grid, sites, state)
    return jnp.mean((predicted - target) ** 2), state


@eqx.filter_jit
def step(log_conductance, state):
    (value, state), gradient = eqx.filter_value_and_grad(loss, has_aux=True)(
        log_conductance, state
    )
    return log_conductance - 0.1 * gradient, value, state


for _ in range(10):
    log_conductance, value, state = step(log_conductance, state)

What the state of each solver keeps from one graph to the next:

Solver Kept by the state GeometricMultigridCGSolver Its preconditioner, the grid; each solve builds the multigrid hierarchy of the new values AMJaxCGSolver Its preconditioner, the prolongation and restriction operators of the algebraic multigrid hierarchy of init; each solve computes the matrices of the coarser levels from the new values CuDSSSolver The analysis, and the factorization while the values stay the same CholmodSolver The last factorization, while the values stay the same Lineax's iterative solvers, such as lineax.CG Nothing: each query runs init

The graphs of one raster shape and contiguity can also share a GridTopology, built once outside jax.jit. It holds their edges, so that each GridGraph(surface, fun=fun, topology=topology) computes its edge weights only.

Windowed analyses build their own states and pass them from tile to tile; see WindowedAnalysis.

docs.title: Extending the solvers
docs.text:
BCOOLinearOperator presents a sparse matrix to Lineax. AbstractSparseSolver is the parent of JAXScape's sparse solvers of symmetric positive definite matrices. Its state holds the compressed sparse row (CSR) sparsity pattern of the matrix, read once from concrete sparse indices, the values, which reinit replaces inside jax.jit, and a factorization or a preconditioner. It scales right-hand sides, checks the sparse indices of each new matrix, and reports failed solves. A new solver subclasses one of its two families, with a final class. The methods that it implements take the sparsity pattern as a CSRPattern: its arrays offsets and columns give the columns of each row, and its properties n, nnz and rows the number of rows, the number of CSR values and the row of each CSR value.

AbstractSparseDirectSolver turns the phases of a sparse factorization library into a solver, and checks each factorization and solve; CuDSSSolver subclasses it:

from typing import final

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape.solvers import AbstractSparseDirectSolver


@final
class MySolver(AbstractSparseDirectSolver):
    def factorize(self, pattern, values):
        return my_library.factorize(pattern.offsets, pattern.columns, values)

    def refactorize(self, factorization, pattern, values):  # Optional.
        return my_library.refactorize(factorization, values)

    def solve(self, factorization, vector):
        return my_library.solve(factorization, vector)

    def residual_tolerance(self, dtype):
        return 1e-4 if dtype == jnp.float64 else 1e-1

The phases run inside jax.jit. Set residual_tolerance from the residuals the library leaves on valid matrices of your workload.

AbstractSparseIterativeSolver runs conjugate gradients with a preconditioner; GeometricMultigridCGSolver and AMJaxCGSolver subclass it. preconditioner builds what the state keeps across values, in init, and precondition returns the preconditioner of the current values at each solve, as a function of residuals. matvec returns the product of the current matrix with vectors, and vector_shape the shape in which both take vectors: csr_matvec multiplies vectors of shape (n,) with the CSR values, and GeometricMultigridCGSolver multiplies rasters with its stencil. Jacobi preconditioning keeps nothing:

from typing import final

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape.solvers import AbstractSparseIterativeSolver, csr_matvec


@final
class JacobiCGSolver(AbstractSparseIterativeSolver):
    rtol: float = 1e-5
    max_steps: int = 1_000

    def preconditioner(self, pattern, values):
        return None

    def precondition(self, preconditioner, pattern, values):
        on_diagonal = jnp.where(pattern.rows == pattern.columns, values, 0)
        diagonal = jnp.zeros(pattern.n, values.dtype).at[pattern.rows].add(on_diagonal)
        return lambda residuals: residuals / diagonal[:, None]

    def matvec(self, preconditioner, pattern, values):
        return csr_matvec(pattern, values)

    def vector_shape(self, preconditioner, pattern):
        return (pattern.n,)

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.operator.BCOOLinearOperator
docs.text:
Lineax linear operator of a jax.experimental.sparse.BCOO matrix.

Its products with vectors are computed with the sparse matrix, so that Lineax solvers that only multiply by the operator, such as lineax.CG, never form a dense matrix. Every BCOOLinearOperator is registered with Lineax as positive semidefinite, whatever its tags, so that lineax.CG accepts it: pass only symmetric positive semidefinite matrices to such solvers.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.sparsesolver.CSRPattern
docs.text:
Compressed sparse row pattern of a BCOO matrix.

Duplicate entries of the BCOO matrix share one CSR value, and its padding entries, whose indices are out of bounds, are left out.

Attributes:

  • offsets: Start of each row in columns, with shape (n + 1,).
  • columns: Column of each CSR value, sorted within each row, with shape (nnz,).
  • value_map: For each stored entry of the BCOO matrix, the index of its CSR value, or nnz for padding entries.
  • max_row_length: Number of CSR values of the longest row. It is static: states whose longest rows differ compile separately.
  • n: Number of rows, and of columns, of the matrix.
  • nnz: Number of CSR values.
  • rows: Row of each CSR value, with shape (nnz,), computed from offsets at each access.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.sparsesolver.AbstractSparseSolver
docs.text:
Lineax solver of sparse symmetric positive definite matrices, with a state for one sparsity pattern.

Subclass AbstractSparseDirectSolver with the phases of a sparse factorization library, or AbstractSparseIterativeSolver with a preconditioner. This class provides what they share. init reads the CSR pattern of the matrix from concrete sparse indices, and reinit replaces its values inside jax.jit, after checking that the sparse indices are those of the pattern. The state holds the pattern, the values, and the factorization or preconditioner of the solver.

Each solve scales the right-hand side exactly, by a power of two, to a largest magnitude in [0.5, 1), so that its solution keeps the precision of the dtype: float32 right-hand sides of about 1e-37 had subnormal solutions. Right-hand sides below the smallest normal number solve to 0. A failed solve returns NaN and reports its failure through lineax.RESULTS, so it raises with throw=True and returns a failed result with throw=False. On GPUs, Lineax may only print the error, and the failed distances are then NaN.

The matrix is symmetric: the state of a solver is also that of the transposed matrix.

Warning

init reads concrete sparse indices: distance.init(graph) builds the state of a GridGraph from its shape and contiguity, also inside jax.jit, and that of another graph outside jax.jit. A state belongs to one sparsity pattern: for a GridGraph, the raster shape and contiguity, with any conductances. reinit raises an error for an operator with other sparse indices.

docs.title: init(operator: AbstractLinearOperator, options: dict[str, typing.Any]) -> State
docs.text:
Return the state of operator, for its sparsity pattern and values.

It reads the sparsity pattern from concrete sparse indices: it raises ValueError for traced sparse indices, as inside jax.jit, and TypeError for an operator that is not BCOO-backed. A solve uses the matrix that its state holds, whatever operator lineax.linear_solve receives: before solving another matrix of the same sparsity pattern, call reinit with its operator.

Arguments:

  • operator: BCOO-backed operator of a symmetric positive definite matrix.
  • options: Unused.

Returns:

The state of operator, which keeps its dtype.

docs.title: reinit(operator: AbstractLinearOperator, options: dict[str, typing.Any], state: State) -> State
docs.text:
Return the state of the values of operator, keeping its pattern.

Arguments:

  • operator: BCOO-backed operator with the sparse indices state was initialized for.
  • options: Unused.
  • state: State from init or an earlier call.

Returns:

The state of the values of operator.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.sparsedirectsolver.AbstractSparseDirectSolver
docs.text:
Direct solver for sparse symmetric positive definite matrices.

Subclass it with the phases of a sparse factorization library: factorize, solve, residual_tolerance and, when the library can reuse an analysis, refactorize. The base class provides the Lineax solver, as AbstractSparseSolver describes: it factorizes the matrix again when its values change, and checks the results.

reinit returns its state itself when the state passed its check and the values are those it factorizes, up to the rounding of assembling the matrix. Otherwise it refactorizes the state, whose factorization may no longer be valid afterwards, and analyses the values afresh when the state failed its check or when the refactorization fails its own.

The checks assume nothing from the library. Each factorization solves A x = A 1, and fails when the backward error max|A 1 - A x| / (||A||_inf max|x|) is not finite or exceeds the square root of the machine epsilon. Each solve fails when its solution x of the scaled right-hand side b is not finite or max|b - A x| exceeds residual_tolerance times max|b|, and reports lineax.RESULTS.singular.

A refactorization that fails its check is retried on a fresh analysis, and the next reinit of a failed state analyses its values afresh, so a failure leaves later values exact. The checks cost one solve of one right-hand side and two sparse matrix-vector products per factorization, and one sparse matrix-vector product per right-hand side.

docs.title: factorize(pattern: CSRPattern, values: Array) -> Factorization
docs.text:
Analyse pattern and factorize values on a new handle.

Arguments:

  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.
  • values: The CSR values of the matrix.

Returns:

A pytree to pass to solve and refactorize, with the same structure for every pattern and values, so that it can pass through jax.lax.cond.

docs.title: refactorize(factorization: Factorization, pattern: CSRPattern, values: Array) -> Factorization
docs.text:
Factorize new values. Defaults to a new analysis with factorize.

Arguments:

  • factorization: A factorization of the same pattern. It need not stay valid after this call.
  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.
  • values: The new CSR values.

Returns:

The factorization of values.

docs.title: solve(factorization: Factorization, vector: Array) -> Array
docs.text:
Solve for one right-hand side, also under jax.vmap over vector.

Arguments:

  • factorization: The factorization of the matrix.
  • vector: The right-hand side, with shape (n,).

Returns:

The solution, with shape (n,).

docs.title: residual_tolerance(dtype: typing.Any) -> float
docs.text:
Largest residual of a solution, relative to its right-hand side.

Arguments:

  • dtype: The dtype of the solution.

Returns:

The tolerance of the infinity norms of the residual and the right-hand side, above the residuals this library leaves on valid matrices.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.sparseiterativesolver.AbstractSparseIterativeSolver
docs.text:
Conjugate gradients on sparse symmetric positive definite matrices, with a preconditioner.

Subclass it with preconditioner, which init builds once, precondition, which applies it to the current values at each solve, matvec, the product of the current matrix with vectors, and vector_shape, the shape of those vectors. csr_matvec gives the product of the CSR values, with vectors of shape (n,). The base class provides the Lineax solver, as AbstractSparseSolver describes: reinit keeps the preconditioner and replaces the values. Values other than those the preconditioner was built from change the number of iterations, and a solve that then exceeds max_steps fails.

A batch of right-hand sides, as jax.vmap makes, runs as one solve with the right-hand sides contiguous in memory, until all have converged. A solve that has not converged after max_steps iterations fails with lineax.RESULTS.max_steps_reached, and one whose solution is not finite, as those of singular matrices can be, with lineax.RESULTS.singular.

Attributes:

  • rtol: Largest Euclidean norm, relative to that of the right-hand side, of the residual that conjugate gradients update at each iteration. In exact arithmetic it equals the residual b - A x of the solution x. In float32, rounding stops the decrease of b - A x, so that solves can converge with a residual b - A x above rtol.
  • max_steps: Largest number of iterations.

docs.title: preconditioner(pattern: CSRPattern, values: Array) -> Preconditioner
docs.text:
Build what the state keeps across values. init calls it.

It may read concrete arrays or run host code, as init runs outside jax.jit, apart from the states that distance.init(graph) builds from the shape and contiguity of a GridGraph, with concrete values. Those build eagerly, under jax.ensure_compile_time_eval, where eqx.error_if raises whatever its condition: it must not call eqx.error_if.

Arguments:

  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.
  • values: The CSR values of the matrix.

Returns:

A pytree, which states carry through jax.jit.

docs.title: precondition(preconditioner: Preconditioner, pattern: CSRPattern, values: Array) -> collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array]
docs.text:
Return the preconditioner of the current values. Each solve calls it once, inside jax.jit.

Arguments:

  • preconditioner: What preconditioner built.
  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.
  • values: The current CSR values of the matrix.

Returns:

A function that applies a symmetric positive definite approximation of the inverse of the matrix to residuals of m right-hand sides, with shape vector_shape(...) + (m,).

docs.title: matvec(preconditioner: Preconditioner, pattern: CSRPattern, values: Array) -> collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array]
docs.text:
Return the product of the matrix with vectors. Each solve calls it once, inside jax.jit. csr_matvec(pattern, values) gives the product of the CSR values.

Arguments:

  • preconditioner: What preconditioner built.
  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.
  • values: The current CSR values of the matrix.

Returns:

A function that multiplies the matrix with m vectors, with shape vector_shape(...) + (m,).

docs.title: vector_shape(preconditioner: Preconditioner, pattern: CSRPattern) -> tuple[int, ...]
docs.text:
Return the shape in which matvec and precondition take vectors: (pattern.n,), or another shape of n entries.

Conjugate gradients carry their vectors in this shape, with a last axis of right-hand sides: a solver of rasters takes them as rasters, which XLA would copy at each iteration if they were reshaped there.

Arguments:

  • preconditioner: What preconditioner built.
  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.

Returns:

A shape of n entries.

docs.title: jaxscape.solvers.sparseiterativesolver.csr_matvec(pattern: CSRPattern, values: Array) -> collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array], jax.Array]
docs.text:
Return the product of the matrix of CSR pattern and values with vectors, as AbstractSparseIterativeSolver.matvec returns it for a vector_shape of (pattern.n,).

It gathers the rows of the matrix when called, and the function it returns reuses them: call it once per solve, as matvec does, and apply the returned function in the loop.

Arguments:

  • pattern: The CSR pattern of the matrix.
  • values: The CSR values of the matrix.

Returns:

A function that multiplies the matrix with m vectors, with shape (n, m).

docs.title: Window operations
docs.text: WindowOperation divides a raster into square core windows that tile it. The total window of a core window adds a buffer of the neighbouring pixels on which a computation on the core window depends. WindowOperation extracts the total windows of a raster and writes the results of a computation on each total window back into a raster, so that computations other than the analyses of Connectivity analysis run as moving-window operations. padding pads a raster to a shape that WindowOperation accepts.

docs.title: jaxscape.window_operation.WindowOperation
docs.text:
Division of a raster into square core windows, each with a buffer.

A large raster is processed one total window at a time. A total window is a core window with its buffer, the band of buffer_size pixels around it, which overlaps the neighbouring total windows: it holds the pixels that a computation on the core window depends on.

Attributes:

  • shape: Raster shape (height, width).
  • window_size: Side of a core window, in pixels.
  • buffer_size: Width of the buffer around each core window, in pixels.
  • total_window_size: Side of a total window, a core window with its buffer, window_size + 2 * buffer_size.
  • x_steps, y_steps: Number of total windows along axis 0, the height, and along axis 1, the width.

Example

import jax.numpy as jnp
from jaxscape import WindowOperation

raster = jnp.ones((100, 100))
window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=raster.shape,
    window_size=20,
    buffer_size=10
)

Warning

shape[i] - 2 * buffer_size must be divisible by window_size along both axes i = 0, 1. jaxscape.utils.padding pads a raster to such a shape.

docs.title: nb_steps property
docs.text:
Number of total windows in the raster.

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
print(window_op.nb_steps)  # 16 (4x4 grid of total windows)

docs.title: extract_total_window(xy: Array, raster: Array) -> Array
docs.text:
Extract a total window, a core window with its buffer, from the raster.

Arguments:

  • xy: Start coordinates [x, y] of the total window.
  • raster: 2D raster array.

Returns:

Total window of shape (total_window_size, total_window_size).

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
raster = jnp.ones((100, 100))
window = window_op.extract_total_window(jnp.array([0, 0]), raster)
# window.shape = (40, 40)

docs.title: extract_core_window(xy: Array, raster: Array) -> Array
docs.text:
Extract a core window, without its buffer, from the raster.

Arguments:

  • xy: Start coordinates [x, y] of the total window.
  • raster: 2D raster array.

Returns:

Core window of shape (window_size, window_size).

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
raster = jnp.ones((100, 100))
core = window_op.extract_core_window(jnp.array([0, 0]), raster)
# core.shape = (20, 20)

docs.title: update_raster_with_core_window(xy: Array, raster: Array, raster_window: Array, fun: collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array, jax.Array], jax.Array] = <lambda>) -> Array
docs.text:
Update a raster with the core window of a processed total window.

Extracts the core window from raster_window and updates the corresponding core window of raster using the provided function.

Arguments:

  • xy: Start coordinates [x, y] of the total window.
  • raster: Full raster array to update.
  • raster_window: Processed total window.
  • fun: Function to combine current and new values. Defaults to replacement.

Returns:

Updated raster array.

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
raster = jnp.zeros((100, 100))

for xy, window in window_op.lazy_iterator(raster):
    processed = compute_distance(window)
    raster = window_op.update_raster_with_core_window(xy, raster, processed)

docs.title: update_raster_with_window(xy: Array, raster: Array, raster_window: Array, fun: collections.abc.Callable[[jax.Array, jax.Array], jax.Array] = <lambda>) -> Array
docs.text:
Update a raster with a whole processed total window.

Arguments:

  • xy: Start coordinates [x, y] of the total window.
  • raster: Full raster array to update.
  • raster_window: Processed total window to merge.
  • fun: Function to combine current and new values. Defaults to replacement.

Returns:

Updated raster array.

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
raster = jnp.zeros((100, 100))
window_data = jnp.ones((40, 40))

# Replace window region
raster = window_op.update_raster_with_window(
    jnp.array([0, 0]), raster, window_data
)

# Accumulate with custom function
raster = window_op.update_raster_with_window(
    jnp.array([0, 0]), raster, window_data, fun=jnp.add
)

docs.title: lazy_iterator(raster: Array) -> collections.abc.Generator[tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array], None, None]
docs.text:
Iterate over the total windows one at a time.

Yields the total windows one after another, so that only one is extracted at a time.

Arguments:

  • raster: 2D raster array to iterate over.

Yields:

Tuples of (xy, window) where xy are start coordinates and window is the extracted total window.

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
raster = jnp.ones((100, 100))

for xy, window in window_op.lazy_iterator(raster):
    # Process each total window sequentially
    result = compute(window)
    # window.shape = (40, 40)

docs.title: eager_iterator(matrix: Array) -> tuple[jax.Array, jax.Array]
docs.text:
Extract all total windows at once, for batched processing.

Extracts the total windows in one operation with jax.vmap, so that a computation can then run on all of them at once.

Arguments:

  • matrix: 2D input raster array.

Returns:

Tuple (xy, windows) where xy has shape (num_windows, 2) containing start coordinates, and windows has shape (num_windows, total_window_size, total_window_size).

Example

window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=(100, 100), window_size=20, buffer_size=10
)
raster = jnp.ones((100, 100))

xy, windows = window_op.eager_iterator(raster)
# xy.shape = (16, 2), windows.shape = (16, 40, 40)

# Process all total windows in parallel
results = jax.vmap(compute)(windows)

docs.title: jaxscape.utils.padding(raster: Array, buffer_size: int, window_size: int) -> Array
docs.text:
Pad raster to a shape that WindowOperation accepts.

Appends rows and columns of zeros at the bottom and right edges, so that (raster.shape[i] - 2 * buffer_size) % window_size == 0 along both axes.

Example

from jaxscape.utils import padding

raster = jnp.ones((100, 100))
padded = padding(raster, buffer_size=10, window_size=25)

docs.title: Benchmark
docs.text: This page compares JAXScape with the software that ecologists use for connectivity analysis on three questions: the distance calculation, the connectivity analysis and the sensitivity analysis. For each tool, it reports the warm runtime and the agreement of the results with a reference. The last section compares the linear solvers of JAXScape. records.csv holds the record of every cell of the run: one setting of a tool on one raster.

docs.title: Hardware and software
docs.text:
• GPU: one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 with 24576 MiB, driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0.
  • CPU: 16 cores of an AMD EPYC 7742 64-Core Processor, under Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS. Each cell runs in its own process, pinned to these cores, with 16 threads for OpenMP, BLAS, Julia and R; XLA sizes its thread pools to the same cores.
  • Languages and libraries: Python 3.13.5, JAX 0.12.0.1, jaxlib 0.12.0.1, PyTorch 2.15.0, Julia 1.13.3, R 4.1.2, Java 21.0.13.

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool Version Questions JAXScape 0.0.16 distance calculation, connectivity analysis, sensitivity analysis Circuitscape.jl 6.1.0 distance calculation ConScape.jl 0.3.0 distance calculation, connectivity analysis, sensitivity analysis gdistance 1.6.5 distance calculation skimage.graph.MCP 0.26.0 distance calculation EcoScape 0.2.5 sensitivity analysis samc 4.2.1 sensitivity analysis eco-connectivity 2.5.0 connectivity analysis Graphab 3.0.8 connectivity analysis Omniscape.jl 0.6.4 sensitivity analysis

The page names the solvers of this run as JAXScape 0.0.18 does: GridMultigridSolver as GeometricMultigridCGSolver.

Parameter mapping of each tool Tool Mapping JAXScape JAXScape builds a GridGraph of the permeability raster with rook contiguity, the conductance of an edge being the harmonic mean of the permeabilities of its two pixels (landscape.conductance), so that its resistance is their mean resistance. The edge cost of least-cost path and free-energy distances is 1 / conductance, and the free-energy distance has the shared theta. The distance calculation is a nodes-to-nodes query among the sites. The connectivity analysis runs SensitivityAnalysis(...).run("quality") for the map and ConnectivityAnalysis for the landscape total, sum_i q_i S_i, and the sensitivity analysis runs SensitivityAnalysis(...).run("permeability"), with the shared dependency_range and coarsening_factor, the default proximity and the batch_size of the settings; these windowed analyses build their graphs with JAXScape's own edge rule, the mean permeability of the two pixels. A proximity setting, a function of the distance in Python such as lambda d: -d, replaces the default proximity. With normalized, the map of the sensitivity analysis is the normalized sensitivity to resistance of the connectivity example: p^2 dC/dp divided by dC/dp on a landscape of permeability 1 and the same quality, and 0 where the latter is not positive, both computed in each call. The distance runs with the solver, the resistance method and the dtype of its settings, such as GeometricMultigridCGSolver(rtol=3e-4) (dense is the dense solve, solver=None), and every call builds the graphs and the solver states. Circuitscape.jl Circuitscape.jl computes the pairwise resistances among the sites of the distance calculation, in its pairwise scenario, with the permeability raster as the conductance of each pixel. connect_four_neighbors_only gives rook contiguity, and connect_using_avg_resistances makes the resistance of an edge the mean resistance of its two pixels, as landscape.conductance does. The solver is cg+amg or cholmod, in double precision, with parallelize on the Julia threads of the cell. Circuitscape.jl has no public in-memory API for this scenario: each call builds its RasterData in memory and runs the internals that compute runs after reading files (build_problem, single_ground_all_pairs), and writes only its table of resistances, to /dev/shm. Every call rebuilds the graph, the Laplacian and the AMG hierarchy or Cholesky factor. ConScape.jl ConScape.jl builds its graph with rook contiguity (N4), the affinity of an edge being the harmonic mean of the permeabilities of its two pixels (AverageWeight), as landscape.conductance gives, and the cost of an edge 1 / affinity (Inv). Its free-energy distance has the shared theta. The distance calculation computes the free-energy distances among the sites, the targets of a GridRSP. ConScape's free-energy distance is directed, and the adapter returns the mean of the two directions between two sites, as JAXScape's FreeEnergyDistance does. The connectivity and sensitivity analyses run on the whole raster, without windows, with targets at landmarks every b pixels (coarse_graining), each holding the quality of its block, where b is the block_size of the windows, JAXScape's block size: 21. The connectivity analysis returns Hanski's S_i, the connected habitat of each pixel at source quality 1 (connected_habitat): the sum over landmarks of their quality times exp(-d / (dependency_range / 4)), exp(-d / 25), for the free-energy distance d to the landmark. The sensitivity analysis returns the quality-weighted betweenness (betweenness_qweighted). JAXScape has no free-energy map, and the configuration compares these maps with JAXScape's under least-cost path distance (compared_with = "lcp"). The free-energy distance tends to a multiple of the resistance distance as theta tends to 0, and to the least-cost path distance as theta grows. On the synthetic raster of 256 pixels a side, for every theta from 1e-5 to 1.5e-2, the ranking of the pairs of sites of the distance calculation by free-energy distance agrees with their ranking by least-cost path distance (Spearman's ρ 0.98 to 0.99, against 0.92 to 0.95 with resistance distance), and at the shared theta, 0.01, ConScape's maps of connectivity and sensitivity correlate more with the maps of JAXScape's GPU cells under least-cost path distance (ρ 0.93 and 0.84) than under resistance distance (0.87 and 0.72). Every call rebuilds the affinities, the Grid, the landmarks and the GridRSP, with its sparse LU factorization, which runs on the BLAS threads of the cell. gdistance gdistance builds a transition layer of the resistance raster, 1 / permeability, with 4 neighbours (rook contiguity) and the transition function 1 / mean(x): the conductance between two pixels is the reciprocal of their mean resistance, landscape.conductance. Resistance distances are commuteDistance divided by the volume of the graph, the sum of its conductances in both directions, and least-cost path distances are costDistance, whose edge cost is 1 / conductance. Pixels have side 1, so geoCorrection leaves the layer unchanged and is left out. Every call builds the transition layer, whose conductances depend on the resistance. skimage.graph.MCP skimage.graph.MCP_Geometric finds least-cost paths on the resistance raster, 1 / permeability, with rook contiguity (fully_connected=False). The cost of a step is the mean resistance of its two pixels, 1 / landscape.conductance, the edge cost of JAXScape. Each call builds the MCP object, and searches from each site until it reaches all the others. EcoScape EcoScape (ecoscape-connectivity) simulates the repopulation of the habitat, the pixels of quality > 0, from seeds drawn at random in it, and maps its flow: the gradient of the repopulation with respect to the permeability of each pixel, times that permeability. Its edge rule is its own: at each step, individuals spread to the 8 neighbours of a pixel, survive a coin toss, and are multiplied by the permeability of their destination. The dispersal distance is the shared dependency_range, in pixels, which is also the border of its tiles and their padding, so that its map covers the raster. Quality enters only as habitat. The other settings are EcoScape's defaults: 400 simulations, 4 seeds per square of side 2 dependency_range + 1, tiles of 1000 pixels and no gap crossing, with the batch_size of the settings and a fixed random seed. EcoScape tiles a raster through GeoTIFFs only: every call writes the habitat and permeability to /dev/shm, runs on the GPU, and reads back the flow, which EcoScape writes with its connectivity. Its map is compared with JAXScape's under least-cost path distances: repopulation follows the most permeable neighbour, the maximum over neighbours, as a least-cost path does. samc samc builds a spatial absorbing Markov chain on the resistance raster, 1 / permeability, with 4 neighbours (rook contiguity) and the transition function 1 / mean(x): an individual moves to a neighbour in proportion to the harmonic mean of the permeabilities of the two pixels, landscape.conductance, and barriers, of permeability 0, are left out of the chain. The absorption of every pixel is (4 / dependency_range)^2 per step, so that an individual moves about dependency_range / 4 pixels before it is absorbed, the length over which JAXScape's default proximity decays. Individuals are released in proportion to quality, and the map is visitation: the expected number of visits to each pixel before absorption. The solver is samc's method, whose direct method factorizes the chain with a single thread. Every call builds the chain, on which samc caches its factorization. Its map is compared with JAXScape's under resistance distances: an absorbing random walk is the random walk behind resistance distance. eco-connectivity eco-connectivity computes the connectedness of each pixel i, with option=1: the sum over pixels j != i of exp(-d(i, j) / 25) q_j, divided by the same sum with quality 1 and every weight 1. Its numerator is Hanski's S_i; its denominator, the reach of an intact landscape, is constant away from the raster's edges. d is a least-cost path distance over 8 neighbours, in which a step costs its length times the weight of the pixel it enters, here its resistance, 1 / permeability: the resistance raster is (r - 1) / (r_max - 1), and max_cost is r_max, the largest resistance. Quality is the condition raster. Barriers, of permeability 0, are masked, and the map is NaN there. Pixels are 1 km, so lambdas=[25] gives the proximity exp(-d/25) in pixels. The multi-resolution graph keeps the default window_size, outer_window and window_mode, and the default levels up to the first whose reach, outer_window times the level in pixels, covers dependency_range. n_threads is the number of cores of the cell. The tool reads GeoTIFFs: each call writes the two rasters to /dev/shm and computes the map from them. Graphab Graphab builds a graph of habitat patches, the clusters of habitat pixels (quality > 0) connected through 4 neighbours. Its links are least-cost paths between patches over 8 neighbours, in which a step costs its length times the mean resistance, 1 / permeability, of its two pixels (extcost), and barriers, of permeability 0, are no data. Links and graph keep the paths of cost up to dependency_range (maxcost, threshold, topo=complete), where the proximity falls to exp(-4). d=25 and p=exp(-1) give the proximity exp(-d/25) on the cost of the shortest path in the graph, which adds the costs of crossing patches. The capacity a_I of a patch is its area in pixels. Each call computes the equivalent connectivity EC of the graph, whose square, the sum over patches I and J of a_I a_J exp(-d_IJ/25), is the landscape total, and the flux F_I = sum over patches J != I of a_J exp(-d_IJ/25) (beta=1). The map is F_I + a_I, the patch analogue of Hanski's S_i, which adds the patch's own term that F leaves out, on the pixels of each patch, and NaN elsewhere. -proc is the number of cores of the cell. Graphab reads and writes files: each call writes the land and resistance rasters to /dev/shm, creates a new project from them, and reads the patches and EC back. Omniscape.jl Omniscape.jl computes the normalized current of the sensitivity analysis with the configuration of its Maryland example: radius is the shared dependency_range, and block_size the side of JAXScape's blocks, dependency_range * coarsening_factor rounded up to an odd integer, 21 pixels. Resistance is 1 / permeability, with the barriers, of permeability 0, as NoData, and the source strength of a pixel is its quality; on Maryland, these are the resistances of the example's reclassification table and the forest sources of its source_from_resistance with r_cutoff 1. The map is the cumulative current divided by the flow potential (calc_normalized_current, calc_flow_potential), compared with JAXScape's normalized sensitivity to resistance, resistance, K = -R, normalized, which the connectivity example relates to it: resistance is the distance of Omniscape's circuits, every pair of habitat pixels has the same weight under the proximity K(R) = -R, as Omniscape injects the current of every source of a window, and the sensitivity is divided by its value on a landscape of permeability 1, as the current is divided by the flow potential. Omniscape keeps its other defaults: eight neighbours, the conductance of an edge being the mean permeability of its two pixels, divided by √2 on diagonals; artifact correction; double precision; the solver of the settings, with the windows solved in parallel on the Julia threads of the cell. Each call runs run_omniscape on arrays in memory, which redoes the sources, the targets and every window solve; it reads and writes no file, and only creates an empty project directory in /dev/shm.

docs.title: Landscapes
docs.text:
• Synthetic rasters of 256², 1024², 4096² and 8192² pixels. The benchmark draws a Gaussian random field \(f\) with a Gaussian covariance of correlation length 25 pixels, on a periodic grid with a fixed seed, and normalizes its ranks to [0, 1]. The habitat quality is \(f\) where \(f \geq 0.7\), and 0 elsewhere: 30 % of the pixels are habitat. The permeability is \(10^{-2(1 - f)}\), from 0.01 to 1, and the resistance is its inverse. A larger raster covers a larger area at the same grain.
  • Maryland, for the connectivity analysis and sensitivity analysis: the land cover of Omniscape's example, the 2016 National Land Cover Database of Frederick, Maryland, 694 × 725 pixels of 30 m. The resistance of each land-cover class is that of Omniscape's reclassification table; medium- and high-intensity development are barriers, and forest, the classes of resistance 1, is habitat of quality 1.

docs.title: Timing
docs.text:
• Warm runtime: the median time of the 5 timed calls of a cell, which follow a warm-up call that compiles the code of the tools that compile; the time of a single timed call when the warm-up call takes more than 5 min.
  • Work of a call: every call redoes the work that depends on the landscape: graph assembly, factorization, multigrid hierarchy and solver state.
  • Speed-up of JAXScape over a tool under a distance: the warm runtime of the tool divided by that of JAXScape on the GPU, each in its fastest setting on the largest synthetic raster that both completed, with JAXScape under the same distance in the distance calculation, and under the distance or label of the column "Compared with JAXScape under" in the connectivity and sensitivity analyses.
  • Time limit: a call stops after 1 h, and in the section of the linear solvers of JAXScape after the time limit stated in its Method.
  • Status of a cell that did not complete: timeout when a call exceeds its time limit, oom when a call runs out of memory, and failed on another error. A setting runs on the synthetic rasters from the smallest up, and is skipped on the rasters larger than one where it stopped; Maryland always runs.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Quantity: the distance \(d_{ij}\) on a graph between habitat sites \(i\) and \(j\): resistance distance, least-cost path distance, and free-energy distance with \(\theta = 0.01\). Ecologists use it in place of Euclidean distance in dispersal kernels and in models of isolation by distance.

  • Graph: every tool builds the same graph: rook contiguity, with the mean resistance of two pixels as the resistance of their edge.
  • Rasters: free-energy distance on 256² and 1024² alone.
  • Error: the largest relative error over the pairs of sites with respect to a float64 reference computed on the CPU: the linear systems of resistance and free-energy distances are solved with JAXScape's CholmodSolver, and least-cost path distances are computed with Dijkstra's algorithm in SciPy.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Quantity: Hanski's connectivity \(S_i = \sum_j K(d_{ij})\, q_j\) of each pixel \(i\), with the habitat quality \(q_j\) of pixel \(j\) and the proximity \(K\), and its landscape total \(C = \sum_i q_i S_i\), the square of the equivalent connected area.
  • JAXScape: in each call, SensitivityAnalysis computes the map of \(\partial C / \partial q_i\), equal to \(2 S_i\) for a symmetric distance, and ConnectivityAnalysis computes \(C\).
  • Windows: windowed analyses with dependency_range 100 pixels and coarsening_factor 0.2, that is, blocks of 21 × 21 pixels, under the proximity \(K(d) = e^{-d/25}\), with \(d\) in equivalent pixels.
  • Graph: rook contiguity, with the mean permeability of two pixels as the conductance of their edge. JAXScape's windowed analyses raise permeability below the permeability floor, a small fraction of the largest permeability, to the floor. On Maryland, the other tools treat the barriers, of permeability 0, as impassable, and JAXScape's analyses still cross the barrier pixels: the edge between a barrier pixel and a pixel of permeability \(p\) has a conductance of about \(p/2\).
  • Resistance distance: SpielmanApproximation(epsilon=0.15) with GeometricMultigridCGSolver(rtol=3e-4), the setting of the connectivity example, on tiles of up to 2,601 block centres.
  • Agreement: Spearman's ρ between the map of a tool and the map of JAXScape on the GPU under the distance or label of the column "Compared with JAXScape under", over the pixels where both maps are defined.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
• Quantity: the sensitivity \(\partial C / \partial p_k\) of \(C\) with respect to the permeability \(p_k\) of each pixel \(k\). The pixels of largest sensitivity are corridors and pinch points: the pixels where a decrease in permeability gives the largest decrease in \(C\).
  • JAXScape: SensitivityAnalysis computes the sensitivity, with the windows and settings of the connectivity analysis. The other tools compute a flow: a current, a betweenness or a number of visits.
  • Normalized sensitivity (K = −R): the map of the section Comparison with Omniscape's normalized current of the connectivity example. Under resistance distance with the proximity \(K(R) = -R\), under which every pair of habitat pixels has the same weight, it is the ratio of \(-\partial C / \partial r_k = p_k^2\, \partial C / \partial p_k\), the sensitivity of \(C\) with respect to the resistance \(r_k\) of pixel \(k\), to its value on a landscape of permeability 1 with the same quality, and 0 where the latter is not positive. Each call computes both sensitivities.
  • Omniscape.jl: computes its normalized current with the configuration of its Maryland example, with radius equal to dependency_range, the same block size, and a graph of eight neighbours.
  • Agreement: as in the connectivity analysis.

• Solvers: JAXScape solves the linear systems of resistance and free-energy distances with one of several solvers, on the GPU, in float32 and float64. dense is the dense solve, solver=None. CholmodSolver factorizes and solves on the CPU.

docs.title: Moving-window operations
docs.text:
In many connectivity measures, the value of a pixel depends on the distances from this pixel to the pixels around it. Computed on the whole raster at once, these distances form a matrix with one row and one column per pixel, which exceeds the memory of common computers for rasters of a few hundred thousand pixels. A moving-window operation divides the raster into square core windows that tile it. The total window of a core window is the core window with a buffer of pixels on every side, so that neighbouring total windows overlap. A function computes the values of the pixels of a core window, its core pixels, from the pixels of its total window, and the core windows are assembled into the output raster. Memory then depends on the size of a total window, and computing time grows linearly with the number of pixels of the raster.

ConnectivityAnalysis and SensitivityAnalysis run moving-window operations internally, for one definition of connectivity. WindowOperation exposes the total windows, so that any function of a total window runs as a moving-window operation. This example computes the area of forest within a given least-cost path distance of each pixel, on the land cover of the connectivity analysis example, and processes the total windows one at a time, then in batches.

Theory: memory and cost of a moving-window operation

A raster of \(n\) pixels has \(n^2\) ordered pairs of pixels. For the \(n = 503{,}150\) pixels of the land cover below, the matrix of the distances between all pairs holds \(2.5 \times 10^{11}\) entries, 1 TB in single precision, and computing it takes at least one operation per entry.

A total window of core width \(w\) and buffer width \(b\) holds \((w + 2b)^2\) pixels. The distances from its \(w^2\) core pixels to all its pixels form a matrix of \(w^2 (w + 2b)^2\) entries, 41 MB in single precision for \(w = 40\) and \(b = 20\). The core windows of about \(n / w^2\) total windows tile the raster, so the moving-window operation computes about \(n (w + 2b)^2\) distances, a number linear in \(n\).

A core pixel lies at least \(b\) pixels from the edge of its total window along each axis. If the value of a pixel is a function of the pixels within \(b\) pixels of it along each axis alone, the moving-window operation returns the same raster as a computation on the whole raster.

docs.title: Land cover, permeability and habitat
docs.text:
The raster holds the classes of the 2016 National Land Cover Database (NLCD) around Frederick, Maryland, in pixels of 30 m. As in the connectivity analysis example, each class is reclassified to a resistance with the table of Omniscape.jl's example.

  • Permeability is the inverse of resistance: 1 in forest, from 1/1000 to 1/20 in other classes, and 0 in medium- and high-intensity development, which are barriers.
  • Habitat quality is 1 in forest and 0 elsewhere.
with rasterio.open(path) as src:
    landcover = src.read(1)

# Resistance of each land cover class, from Omniscape's example; inf for barriers
resistance_table = {
    11: 100,  # Open water
    21: 500,  # Developed, open space
    22: 1000,  # Developed, low intensity
    23: np.inf,  # Developed, medium intensity
    24: np.inf,  # Developed, high intensity
    31: 100,  # Barren land
    41: 1,  # Deciduous forest
    42: 1,  # Evergreen forest
    43: 1,  # Mixed forest
    52: 20,  # Shrub/scrub
    71: 30,  # Grassland/herbaceous
    81: 200,  # Pasture/hay
    82: 300,  # Cultivated crops
    90: 20,  # Woody wetlands
    95: 30,  # Emergent herbaceous wetlands
}
lookup = np.full(256, np.nan)
for nlcd_class, value in resistance_table.items():
    lookup[nlcd_class] = value
resistance = lookup[landcover]

permeability = jnp.asarray(1 / resistance, dtype="float32")  # 0 for barriers
quality = jnp.asarray(resistance == 1, dtype="float32")  # Forest
barrier = np.isinf(resistance)
print(f"{quality.size:,} pixels: {quality.mean():.0%} forest")
print(f"{barrier.mean():.0%} barriers")

docs.title: Core windows and total windows
docs.text:
The raster is divided into core windows, each at the centre of its total window. The buffer width \(b\) is set by the range of the computed value, and the core width \(w\) by the memory available for one total window.

Here, the value of a pixel is the area of forest within a least-cost path distance \(d_\text{max} = 20\) of it, the cost of 20 steps between forest pixels (600 m). The buffer is \(b = d_\text{max} = 20\) pixels wide (see the theory box of the next section). With core windows of \(w = 40\) pixels, the total windows have 80 x 80 pixels.

WindowOperation requires the height and the width of the raster, minus \(2b\), to be multiples of \(w\). The rasters are padded with \(b\) pixels on every side, so that every pixel of the raster lies in a core window, then padding pads their bottom and right edges to the next multiple. Padding pixels have permeability 0 and quality 0.

d_max = 20  # Least-cost path distance within which forest is counted
buffer_size = d_max  # Buffer width b, in pixels
window_size = 40  # Core width w, in pixels


def pad(raster):
    # b pixels on every side, then the bottom and right edges to fit the cores
    return padding(jnp.pad(raster, buffer_size), buffer_size, window_size)


permeability_padded = pad(permeability)
quality_padded = pad(quality)
window_op = WindowOperation(
    shape=permeability_padded.shape, window_size=window_size, buffer_size=buffer_size
)

height, width = quality.shape
side = window_op.total_window_size
print(f"Raster of {height} x {width} pixels, padded to {quality_padded.shape}")
print(f"{window_op.nb_steps} total windows of {side} x {side} pixels")

docs.title: Reachable forest in one total window
docs.text:
The function computed in each total window gives, for each core pixel, the area of forest within a least-cost path distance \(d_\text{max}\) of it.

A GridGraph is built from the permeability of a total window: its edges join each pixel to its four neighbours, and the conductance of an edge is the mean permeability of its two pixels. LCPDistance computes least-cost path distances, where the cost of an edge of conductance \(a\) is \(1/a\). Its method sources_to_windows_distance returns the distances from each core pixel to the pixels of the square of side \(2 d_\text{max} + 1\) centred on it, its window. The function counts the forest pixels of each window at a distance of at most \(d_\text{max}\), and multiplies the count by the area of a pixel, 0.09 hectares (ha).

Theory: why the moving-window result is exact

Permeability is at most 1, so the cost of every edge is at least 1, the cost of a step between two forest pixels. A path of cost at most \(d_\text{max}\) therefore has at most \(d_\text{max}\) edges, and stays within \(d_\text{max}\) pixels of its source along each axis. With \(b \geq d_\text{max}\), every such path from a core pixel lies inside the total window and inside the window of the pixel. Least-cost path distances on the graph of the total window then equal those on the graph of the whole raster wherever the latter are at most \(d_\text{max}\), and exceed \(d_\text{max}\) elsewhere: the moving-window operation returns the same raster as a computation on the whole raster.

The resistance distance depends on all paths between two pixels, including those that leave the total window, and has no such bound. For such distances, with a wider buffer, the error of the moving-window operation is smaller and its cost larger.

distance = LCPDistance()
size = 2 * d_max + 1  # Side of the window of a pixel
pixel_area = 0.09  # Hectares, for pixels of 30 m


def average(x, y):
    return (x + y) / 2


def reachable_forest(permeability, quality, rows, columns):
    # Area of forest, in hectares, within a least-cost path distance d_max of
    # the pixels at `rows` and `columns`
    graph = GridGraph(permeability, fun=average)
    sources = graph.coord_to_index(rows, columns)
    distances = distance.sources_to_windows_distance(graph, sources, size)
    forest = jax.vmap(
        lambda row, column: lax.dynamic_slice(
            quality, (row - d_max, column - d_max), (size, size)
        )
    )(rows, columns)
    return pixel_area * jnp.sum((distances <= d_max) * forest, axis=(1, 2))


# Rows and columns of the core pixels in a total window
core = jnp.arange(buffer_size, buffer_size + window_size)
core_rows, core_columns = (x.ravel() for x in jnp.meshgrid(core, core, indexing="ij"))


@jax.jit
def process_window(permeability_window, quality_window):
    area = reachable_forest(
        permeability_window, quality_window, core_rows, core_columns
    )
    # A raster of the shape of the total window, whose buffer the update discards
    return jnp.pad(area.reshape(window_size, window_size), buffer_size)

docs.title: Processing total windows one at a time
docs.text:
lazy_iterator yields the total windows of a raster one at a time, with the row and column xy of their top-left pixel in the padded raster. extract_total_window extracts the total window of the quality raster at the same position, and update_raster_with_core_window writes the core window of the result into the output raster. The distances of one total window, from 1,600 core pixels to 6,400 pixels, take 41 MB. The time below includes the compilation of process_window.

start = time.perf_counter()
lazy = jnp.zeros_like(quality_padded)
for xy, permeability_window in window_op.lazy_iterator(permeability_padded):
    quality_window = window_op.extract_total_window(xy, quality_padded)
    result = process_window(permeability_window, quality_window)
    lazy = window_op.update_raster_with_core_window(xy, lazy, result)
lazy = jax.block_until_ready(lazy)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"{window_op.nb_steps} total windows, one at a time: {elapsed:.1f} s")

342 total windows, one at a time: 10.5 s

docs.title: Processing total windows in batches
docs.text:
eager_iterator returns all total windows of a raster at once, in an array of shape (total windows, w + 2b, w + 2b), with their positions, for functions that process many total windows in one program. jax.lax.map with batch_size=32 applies process_window, vectorized with jax.vmap, to batches of 32 total windows. Memory holds all total windows, about \((1 + 2b/w)^2 = 4\) times the padded raster, and the distances of one batch, 1.3 GB. The time below includes compilation.

start = time.perf_counter()
xy, permeability_windows = window_op.eager_iterator(permeability_padded)
_, quality_windows = window_op.eager_iterator(quality_padded)
results = lax.map(
    lambda windows: process_window(*windows),
    (permeability_windows, quality_windows),
    batch_size=32,
)
eager = jnp.zeros_like(quality_padded)
for xy_window, result in zip(xy, results):
    eager = window_op.update_raster_with_core_window(xy_window, eager, result)
eager = jax.block_until_ready(eager)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
print(f"Total windows of shape {permeability_windows.shape}")
print(f"{window_op.nb_steps} total windows, in batches of 32: {elapsed:.1f} s")
print(f"Largest difference between the two rasters: {jnp.max(jnp.abs(eager - lazy))}")

docs.title: Connectivity analysis
docs.text:
A connectivity analysis quantifies how much habitat a species can reach, given the resistance of the landscape to its movement. JAXScape measures it by the connectivity

\[C = \sum_i \sum_{j \neq i} q_i \, K_{ij} \, q_j,\]

where \(q_i\) is the habitat quality of pixel \(i\) and \(K_{ij}\) is the proximity of pixels \(i\) and \(j\): a dispersal kernel that decreases with a distance \(d_{ij}\), which grows with the resistance (the inverse of the permeability \(p\)) of the pixels between them. Maps of the sensitivities of \(C\), its derivatives with respect to the permeability \(p_k\) and the habitat quality \(q_k\) of each pixel \(k\), show where a gain in permeability or in habitat most increases the habitat that the species can reach. The elasticities express the same derivatives in relative terms.

This example computes \(C\) with ConnectivityAnalysis and its sensitivities with SensitivityAnalysis, on the 2016 land cover around Frederick, Maryland, with forest as the habitat, for two distances: the least-cost path distance and the resistance distance.

docs.title: Land cover, habitat quality and permeability
docs.text:
The analyses take two rasters of the same shape: the habitat quality \(q\) and the permeability \(p\) of each pixel. Both derive here from the classes of the 2016 National Land Cover Database (NLCD), in pixels of 30 m, through the resistances of Omniscape.jl's example on the same raster.

  • Habitat quality is 1 in forest, the land cover of resistance 1, and 0 elsewhere.
  • Permeability is the inverse of the resistance: 1 in forest, down to 1/1000 in low-intensity development. Medium- and high-intensity development are barriers, of infinite resistance and permeability 0. The analyses raise every permeability below the permeability floor, \(10^{-4}\) times the largest permeability, to that floor: barriers are nearly impassable, and the graph of every window stays connected.
